Chapter 9 · 第九章

Managing Technical Projects管理技术项目

— PDF p.283 —

No matter how strong your technical skills are, stepping into a tech lead role means entering a new layer of complexity, one where communication, prioritization, and expectation management matter just as much as architecture and code.

无论你的技术功底多扎实，走上技术负责人（tech lead）岗位都意味着进入一个全新的复杂层级——在这里，沟通、优先级排序和预期管理，与架构设计和写代码同等重要。

From my experience, your biggest challenges won’t be technical. They’ll come from aligning people, managing expectations, and keeping your team on track when things inevitably shift.

以我的经验来看，你面临的最大挑战不会是技术问题，而是让众人对齐、管理预期，以及在事情不可避免地发生变化时让团队不脱轨。

In this chapter, I’ll share practical ways to lead through that complexity. I start with how to define a clear technical vision and shape a strategy to achieve it. Then, I’ll cover how to help your team make thoughtful technical decisions that align with that vision. Finally, I’ll walk through how to track key decisions over time using tools like architecture decision records (ADRs).

在本章中，我会分享带领团队穿越这种复杂性的实用方法。我先讲如何定义清晰的技术愿景，并塑造实现它的战略；然后讲如何帮助团队做出与该愿景一致、深思熟虑的技术决策；最后讲如何用架构决策记录（ADR）之类的工具，随时间追踪关键决策。

Next, I focus on how to encourage technical excellence inside your team. I’ll talk about what it means to define team standards, how to build fast feedback loops into your delivery pipeline, how to measure what matters, and how to ensure quality through meaningful, useful testing practices.

接下来，我聚焦于如何在团队内部鼓励技术卓越。我会谈及定义团队标准意味着什么、如何在交付流水线中构建快速反馈回路、如何度量真正重要的东西，以及如何通过有意义、有用的测试实践来保障质量。

Finally, I’ll walk through four of the most common project management challenges I’ve seen tech leads face: planning and keeping a project on track, dealing with delays when the plan goes off course, balancing multiple streams of work at once, and identifying and managing technical risks before they escalate.

最后，我会逐一讲解我所见过的技术负责人最常遇到的四类项目管理挑战：规划并让项目不脱轨、在计划偏离正轨时应对延期、同时平衡多条工作流，以及在技术风险升级之前识别并管理它们。

This chapter is about leading with clarity. You won’t always get everything right, but the more proactive, transparent, and collaborative you are in how you lead projects, the more trust you’ll build, and the stronger your team’s delivery will become.

本章的核心是"以清晰引领"。你不可能事事都做对，但你在带领项目时越主动、越透明、越协作，建立的信任就越多，团队的交付能力也就越强。

— PDF p.284 —

Aligning Your Team on a Common Tech Strategy让团队在统一技术战略上对齐

Most problems in tech teams come from people not being properly aligned. Even worse is when everyone thinks they’re aligned, but they actually aren’t. That’s how you end up with a feature that takes a month to build and turns out completely different from what the business expected.

技术团队里的大多数问题，都源于人们没有真正对齐。更糟的是，人人都以为自己对齐了，其实并没有。于是就会出现这种情况：一个功能开发了一个月，结果与业务方的预期完全不同。

I’ve seen it happen so many times.

这种事我见过太多次了。

You might be thinking, "But didn’t they talk along the way? Didn’t they have check-ins, showcases?" Well, yes. Communication happened, but everyone was so sure they were on the same page that they missed the red flags, until the product was in front of stakeholders, and it was obvious it wasn’t what they needed.

你可能会想："可他们一路上没沟通吗？没开过同步会、没做过演示吗？"嗯，都有。沟通确实发生了，但每个人都太确信大家步调一致，以至于忽略了危险信号——直到产品摆在利益相关者面前，才明显看出这不是他们要的东西。

Misalignment always comes down to poor communication between the people involved. And bad communication doesn’t just happen at the start; it follows through the whole process. It’s usually only when the damage is clear that people realize something went wrong.

不对齐，归根结底都是相关人员之间沟通不畅。而糟糕的沟通不只发生在开头，它贯穿整个过程。通常只有在损害已经显而易见时，人们才意识到哪里出了问题。

Clear alignment means everyone knows why you’re building something, has a shared high-level understanding of how, and has agreed on a rough timeline. Clear, written alignment brings commitment.

清晰的对齐意味着：每个人都知道你为什么要做某件事，对"怎么做"有共同的高层理解，并且对大致时间表达成一致。清晰的、书面化的对齐，才能带来承诺。

This is where your role as a tech lead becomes crucial. You’re standing at the intersection between your team and the business, responsible for keeping everyone aligned and committed. Your team will be making a lot of decisions, technical and not, and you’ll be right in the middle of that process, ensuring that both sides understand each other clearly.

这时你作为技术负责人的角色就至关重要了。你站在团队与业务的交汇处，负责让所有人保持对齐和承诺。你的团队会做出大量决策——技术的和非技术的——而你正处在这个过程的中央，确保双方都清楚地理解彼此。

To do this well, you need enough technical depth to guide your team’s work, and the communication skills to translate risks, problems, and strategies back to your stakeholders, whether they’re deeply technical or not.

要把这件事做好，你既需要足够的技术深度来指导团队的工作，也需要沟通能力，把风险、问题和战略"翻译"给你的利益相关者——无论他们本身是否精通技术。

In this section, I’ll focus on the skills you need to develop and practical strategies you can use to help your team make technical decisions smoothly, take decision making to the next level by building a shared technical vision, and document decisions clearly to ensure long-term commitment.

在本节中，我会聚焦于你需要培养的技能，以及可以使用的实用策略：帮助团队顺畅地做出技术决策、通过建立共享的技术愿景把决策提升到新的高度，并把决策清晰地记录下来，以确保长期的承诺。

Even though the examples will focus on technical decisions, the same strategies easily apply to any type of decision your team needs to make.

尽管例子会聚焦于技术决策，但同样的策略也很容易适用于团队需要做的任何类型的决策。

— PDF p.285 —

Build a Technical Vision (and Turn It into a Strategy)构建技术愿景（并把它转化为战略）

As a tech lead, one of your most impactful responsibilities is helping your team define a clear technical vision, then shaping a strategy that turns that vision into reality.

作为技术负责人，你最有影响力的职责之一，就是帮助团队定义清晰的技术愿景，然后塑造一套把愿景变为现实的战略。

A technical vision describes what "good" looks like for your team’s technology. It’s aspirational and directional. It defines your north star: the destination you’re heading toward.

技术愿景描述的是：对团队的技术而言，"好"是什么样子。它是理想化的、有方向感的。它定义了你的北极星：你正在朝往的目的地。

Example: "We want a resilient and maintainable architecture that allows any developer to safely deploy to production in under 10 minutes."

示例："我们希望拥有一套弹性且可维护的架构，让任何开发者都能在 10 分钟内安全地部署到生产环境。"

A technical strategy, on the other hand, is the plan for how you’ll get there. It outlines concrete steps and trade-offs based on where you’re starting, the resources you have, and the constraints you’re working with.

而技术战略，则是你如何到达那里的计划。它根据你的起点、你拥有的资源、以及你身处的约束，勾勒出具体的步骤和权衡。

Example: "We’ll break our monolith into services starting with billing, adopt feature flags for safer deployments, and implement observability dashboards to surface errors faster."

示例："我们将从计费模块开始，把单体系统拆分为服务；采用 feature flag（特性开关）以实现更安全的部署；并搭建可观测性仪表盘，让错误更快地显现出来。"

A helpful analogy here is building a house:

这里有一个很贴切的类比——盖房子：

  • The business strategy is why you’re building it. Maybe it’s to house a growing family, create a coworking space, or sell it as an investment. It sets the purpose and defines success.业务战略，是你为什么要盖它。也许是为了容纳一个不断壮大的家庭、打造一个联合办公空间，或者作为投资品出售。它确立目的，定义什么是成功。
  • The technical vision is the blueprint of the finished house: the overall design and feel. It shows that you want a two-story home with lots of natural light, an open kitchen, energy-efficient systems, and room to expand. It captures what "good" looks like when it’s done.技术愿景，是完工后房子的蓝图：整体设计与观感。它表明你想要一栋采光充足的两层住宅、开放式厨房、节能系统，以及可扩展的空间。它捕捉的是"完工时好是什么样"。
  • The technical strategy is the construction plan: how you’ll build it, in what order, and with what constraints. Maybe you’ll use modular construction to speed things up, reuse the foundation of an older building, or phase the work so you finish the essential rooms first. It reflects how you’ll get there, given your tools, timeline, and budget.技术战略，是施工计划：你将怎么盖、按什么顺序盖、在什么约束下盖。也许你会用模块化施工来加快速度、复用一栋老建筑的地基，或者分阶段施工、先把关键房间盖好。它反映的是：在给定工具、工期和预算的条件下，你如何到达那里。
  • Tactics are the daily site decisions: what to fix today, which materials to use for the flooring, or how to respond when it rains and delays the roof.战术，则是工地上的日常决策：今天修哪里、地板用什么材料、下雨延误了屋顶工程怎么办。
— PDF p.286 —

Vision gives you the why and where. Strategy gives you the how. Both are essential. Without vision, you risk building in circles. Without strategy, you may never get to your destination, or go wildly over budget.

愿景给你"为什么"和"去哪里"，战略给你"怎么做"。两者都不可或缺。没有愿景，你可能在原地兜圈子；没有战略，你可能永远到不了目的地，或者彻底超支。

Before starting to work toward a direction, you need to assess your current context:

在朝某个方向发力之前，你需要先评估当前的处境：

  • Business goals: What’s the product aiming to achieve?业务目标：产品想达成什么？
  • Team strengths and skills: What technologies are they confident in?团队优势与技能：他们对哪些技术最有把握？
  • Cross-functional requirements: Performance, observability, security?跨职能需求：性能、可观测性、安全性？
  • Team shape: What complexity can your current size and roles support?团队形态：以你现有的规模和角色，能支撑多大的复杂度？
  • Tech landscape: What are you already using? What’s working?技术格局：你们已经在用什么？哪些运行良好？

There’s a concept I find useful here: enabling constraints. Your vision and strategy have to live within the bounds of your company’s reality, like a requirement to use Ruby on Rails or stick with monolithic deployment. Ignoring these constraints leads to frustration when decisions made by the team turn out to be impossible due to external limitations.

这里有一个我觉得很有用的概念：赋能型约束（enabling constraints）。你的愿景和战略必须落在公司现实的边界之内，比如"必须使用 Ruby on Rails"或"坚持单体部署"。如果无视这些约束，当团队做出的决策因外部限制而根本无法落地时，就会非常挫败。

Instead, make these constraints visible early. Set the boundaries clearly so the vision is grounded, realistic, and actionable.

相反，要尽早让这些约束浮出水面。把边界划清楚，让愿景脚踏实地、现实可行、可以执行。

For both vision and strategy, visualization is required as it transforms these from an idea to something tangible you can work with.

无论是愿景还是战略，都需要可视化——因为可视化能把它们从一个想法，变成你可以着手处理的、有形的东西。

Both can be a simple document or a visual board (e.g., a Mural board) containing different artifacts like the following:

两者都可以是一份简单的文档，或一块可视化白板（例如 Mural 看板），里面包含如下各种制品：

  • Architecture diagrams; you can use the C4 model (more in the section "Visualizing a System Architecture" on page 226)架构图；你可以使用 C4 模型（详见第 226 页"可视化系统架构"一节）
  • Path to production (more in the section "Defining Your Path to Production" on page 239)通往生产环境的路径（详见第 239 页"定义你的交付路径"一节）
  • Cross-functional requirements (more in the section "Defining and Managing Cross-Functional Requirements" on page 232)跨职能需求（详见第 232 页"定义与管理跨职能需求"一节）
— PDF p.287 —
  • Test or quality strategy documents (more in the section "Continuously Testing" on page 245)测试或质量战略文档（详见第 245 页"持续测试"一节）
  • Ways of working processes (more in the section "How to Build a Healthy Team Culture" on page 185)工作方式与流程（详见第 185 页"如何打造健康的团队文化"一节）

Not every team needs all of these; start with what’s most relevant for your context. For example, you might use architecture diagrams to illustrate both your vision (the future state) and your strategy (the incremental stages to get there).

并非每个团队都需要全部这些；从与你处境最相关的开始。例如，你可以用架构图同时展示你的愿景（未来状态）和战略（到达那里的各个增量阶段）。

Tip: If you’re interested in a deeper breakdown of technical vision versus strategy, examples, and more resources on how to build them, I highly recommend the chapter "What’s a Vision? What’s a Strategy?" in The Staff Engineer’s Path by Tanya Reilly (O’Reilly).

提示：如果你想更深入地了解技术愿景与战略的区别、示例，以及更多如何构建它们的资源，我强烈推荐 Tanya Reilly 所著《The Staff Engineer’s Path》（O’Reilly 出版）中的"What’s a Vision? What’s a Strategy?"一章。

When you’ve articulated both the why/where (vision) and the how (strategy), execution becomes a lot smoother. To bring the strategy to life, you’ll want to do the following:

当你把"为什么/去哪里"（愿景）和"怎么做"（战略）都讲清楚之后，执行就会顺畅得多。要让战略落地，你需要做到以下几点：

  • Break down initiatives into clear milestones: These should represent visible progress: things you can demo, ship, or measure.把举措拆解为清晰的里程碑：这些里程碑应当代表可见的进展——你可以演示、发布或度量的东西。
  • Connect strategy to the backlog: If your vision includes improving reliability, that should translate into specific tasks: refactoring flaky tests, improving alerting, or addressing known error patterns.把战略与待办列表（backlog）连接起来：如果你的愿景包含提升可靠性，那就应当转化为具体任务：重构不稳定的测试、改进告警，或处理已知的错误模式。
  • Create feedback loops: Set regular checkpoints, like weekly syncs, quarterly reviews, or retrospectives, to assess whether you’re on track, what’s been learned, and what needs to change.建立反馈回路：设定定期检查点，比如每周同步会、季度评审或回顾会，用以评估你是否走在正轨上、学到了什么、以及需要改变什么。
  • Track and communicate progress: Share updates regularly. Keep stakeholders aligned, and make it easy for the team to know what’s moving forward, what’s blocked, and where help is needed. Don’t just focus on what’s done; highlight the impact and tie it back to the vision.追踪并沟通进展：定期分享更新。让利益相关者保持对齐，并让团队容易看清什么在推进、什么被阻塞、哪里需要帮助。不要只关注"做完了什么"；要突出影响，并把它和愿景关联起来。
— PDF p.288 —
  • Celebrate alignment in action: When a team makes a decision that reflects the technical vision, like choosing a simpler solution because it aligns with the goal of maintainability, call it out.赞美"落到实处的对齐"：当团队做出一个体现技术愿景的决策时——比如因为符合可维护性目标而选择了更简单的方案——要把它点出来、给予肯定。

Conclusion: Vision gives you direction. Strategy gives you a path. Execution turns ideas into impact.

小结：愿景给你方向，战略给你路径，执行把想法变成影响。

Help Your Team Make Technical Decisions帮助团队做出技术决策

Once you have agreed on a plan with your team, the next challenge is making daily technical decisions that move you toward that direction. As a tech lead, you’ll be involved in decision making constantly.

一旦和团队就计划达成一致，下一个挑战就是：做出日复一日、能把你推向那个方向的技术决策。作为技术负责人，你会不断地参与决策。

Whether it’s choosing between libraries, deciding how to integrate a new feature, or debating between building in-house versus buying off the shelf, your role is to support the team in making thoughtful, informed, and aligned decisions. You’re there to guide the process, facilitate the conversations, and help the team weigh trade-offs.

无论是在多个库之间做选择、决定如何集成一个新功能，还是在"自研"与"采购现成方案"之间权衡，你的角色都是支持团队做出深思熟虑、知情且对齐的决策。你在那里是为了引导流程、主持对话，并帮助团队权衡取舍。

The first thing is to make sure your team is clear on how decisions are made. Having an open conversation about your decision-making process can eliminate wrong assumptions. Many people are surprised when I tell them I won’t make all decisions, that I want and expect them to contribute.

第一件事，是确保你的团队清楚决策是如何做出的。就你的决策方式进行一次公开对话，可以消除错误的假设。当我告诉大家"我不会把所有决策都自己做，我希望也期待你们贡献想法"时，很多人都感到意外。

There are different decision-making styles out there. The most common ones are autocratic, consultative, democratic, and consensus (explained in Table 9-1). Each approach has its pros and cons and works better for certain types of decisions.

决策风格有很多种。最常见的是：专制式（autocratic）、协商式（consultative）、民主式（democratic）和共识式（consensus）（见表 9-1）。每种方式都有其优缺点，适用于不同类型的决策。

A note on consensus: consensus doesn’t mean everyone has to agree 100% or love the decision. In practice, it often means everyone is willing to support the outcome and move forward, even if it’s not their personal preference. This is sometimes called consent. People may not feel strongly in favor, but they don’t strongly object either. Clarifying this up front can help avoid endless debates and make consensus-based decisions more effective in practice.

关于共识式要说明一点：共识并不意味着每个人都要 100% 同意或都喜欢这个决定。在实践中，它往往意味着：每个人都愿意支持这个结果并继续前进，即便这不是他们个人的偏好。这有时被称为"同意（consent）"。人们可能并不强烈赞同，但也不强烈反对。事先把这一点讲清楚，可以避免无休止的争论，让基于共识的决策在实践中更有效。

— PDF p.289 —

— PDF p.290 —

All of these decision-making styles are valid options based on the problem at hand. Problems start when you overuse one approach because it’s more comfortable. My invitation here is: notice your tendency. Are you stuck using just one method?

根据面对的问题，以上这些决策风格都是有效的选择。当你因为某一种方式更顺手而过度使用它时，问题就来了。我在这里想提醒你：留意自己的惯性。你是不是困在只用某一种方法上？

Starting tech leads often fall into the trap of making all the decisions themselves. Maybe they feel pressure to know everything or think it’s their job because they’re accountable. But this creates bottlenecks, slows down the team, and reduces people’s growth, including your own.

初任技术负责人常常掉进"所有决策都自己做"的陷阱。也许他们觉得有压力、必须什么都懂，或者因为自己要担责就觉得这是自己的活。但这会制造瓶颈、拖慢团队，并抑制大家的成长——包括你自己。

At the other extreme, when I started leading, I tried too hard to involve everyone. Every decision became a team discussion. I wanted to avoid being the leader who made all decisions alone, but in doing that, I slowed us down and frustrated my team. It took forever to reach consensus.

在另一个极端，我刚开始带人时，则过度地想让每个人都参与。每个决策都变成一场团队讨论。我想避免成为那种独自拍板的领导，但这样做反而拖慢了我们，也让团队很挫败。达成共识要花上好久。

And then, under pressure, when I finally made a unilateral decision, people were relieved. That taught me: the problem isn’t the decision style. The problem is staying stuck at one extreme. Balance comes from knowing when to involve everyone and when to make the call yourself.

后来，在压力之下我终于单方面拍板时，大家反而松了一口气。这让我明白：问题不在于决策风格，而在于困在某一个极端不动。平衡来自于知道何时让大家都参与、何时由自己拍板。

The main thing that would have helped? Setting expectations up front. Let your team know how you plan to make decisions based on the context, whether you’ll consult, involve, or decide quickly under time pressure.

最有帮助的做法是什么？事先把预期讲清楚。让团队知道：你会根据具体情境如何决策——是会咨询大家、让大家参与，还是在时间压力下快速决定。

This isn’t rare. I was not the only one falling into this trap. I still see and work with tech leads every day who struggle with finding the right balance between making decisions themselves and involving their team. Just make sure you’re using all the tools the role gives you. Build awareness of the options you have.

这种情况并不少见。掉进这个陷阱的不只我一个。我现在每天仍会遇到并与这样的技术负责人共事：他们在"自己拍板"和"让团队参与"之间难以找到恰当的平衡。只要确保你把这个角色赋予你的所有工具都用起来就行。去建立对自己可选方案的觉察。

In general, you should aim toward group-oriented decision making whenever possible. Involving people leads to higher commitment and better results. And the most common way we have these days to make decisions as a group is through meetings. The bigger the decision, the bigger the meeting (more people involved). To make these decision-making meetings effective, you need strong facilitation skills.

总体而言，只要有可能，你就应当尽量倾向于群体式决策。让大家参与会带来更高的承诺度和更好的结果。而如今我们作为群体做决策最常见的方式，就是开会。决策越大，会议就越大（参与的人越多）。要让这些决策会议有效，你需要很强的主持（facilitation）技巧。

Table 9-2 is a practical guide to the most common meeting pitfalls and what you can do about them in the role of facilitator.

表 9-2 是一份实用指南，列出了最常见的会议陷阱，以及作为主持人你可以如何应对。

— PDF p.291 —
Common problem
常见问题		Why it’s a problem
为什么是问题		How to address it
如何应对
No clear goal
目标不清晰		• Meeting feels pointless.
• 会议让人觉得毫无意义。

• People don’t know what’s expected.
• 大家不知道期待自己做什么。

• Time is wasted.
• 时间被浪费。		• Name meetings clearly ("Define delivery strategy for X" instead of "Talk about X").
• 会议命名要清晰（用"定义 X 的交付战略"，而不是"聊聊 X"）。

• Add a description with meeting goals and links.
• 在描述里写明会议目标并附上链接。

• Start the meeting by stating the goal.
• 开场先复述会议目标。
Meeting keeps derailing
会议不断跑偏		• Conversation goes off-topic.
• 讨论跑题。

• Important discussions are missed.
• 重要的讨论被漏掉。

• Meeting feels chaotic.
• 会议一团乱。		• Anchor the conversation: "How is this helping us reach our goal?", "Is this relevant for the conversation?"
• 把讨论"锚定"回来："这对我们达成目标有什么帮助？""这与当前讨论相关吗？"

• Use whiteboarding (e.g., FigJam) to track the discussion live.
• 用白板（如 FigJam）实时记录讨论。

• Split big problems into smaller pieces if needed.
• 必要时把大问题拆成小块。

• Use RAID board to capture risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies.
• 用 RAID 看板记录风险（risks）、假设（assumptions）、问题（issues）、依赖（dependencies）。
Loud voices dominate
声音大的人主导		Only a few opinions are heard, and valuable ideas from quieter team members are missed.
只有少数意见被听到，安静成员的宝贵想法被忽略。		• "Pass the microphone": invite quieter voices to speak.
• "把话筒传出去"：邀请安静的人发言。

• Use different tools to gather inputs: besides everyone sharing their idea out loud, you can use tools like anonymous forms, one-on-ones, or even write it down on Post-its.
• 用不同工具收集意见：除了让大家大声说出想法，还可以用匿名表单、一对一沟通，甚至写在便签上。

• Remote: make considerate use of the hands-up and chat features in your video conferencing tool.
• 远程时：体贴地用好视频会议工具里的"举手"和"聊天"功能。
Constant interruptions
不断被打断		• Hard to get your point across.
• 很难把话说完。

• Conversations lose focus and energy.
• 讨论失去焦点和劲头。

• People interrupted get demotivated and less engaged as they don’t feel listened to.
• 被打断的人会因感觉不被倾听而失去动力、参与度下降。		• If you are interrupted, politely but firmly say, "I’m not finished speaking," "as I was saying before."
• 如果你被打断，礼貌而坚定地说："我还没说完""我刚才说到……"。

• If someone else is interrupted, as a facilitator you have the power to bring that interrupted voice back: "Maria, I think you were saying something on this topic before?"
• 如果别人被打断，作为主持人你有权把那个被打断的声音请回来："Maria，你刚才好像正要就这个话题说点什么？"

• Create a rule to speak: raise your hand and ensure all raised hands are listened to.
• 立一条发言规则：举手发言，并确保所有举手的人都被听到。
Meeting drags on too long
会议拖太久		Rushed decisions and fatigue.
决策仓促、人也疲惫。		• Assign a timekeeper.
• 指定计时员。

• Split the meeting into timed sections.
• 把会议切成计时的若干段。

• Do time checks ("15 minutes left. Do you want to continue on this topic?").
• 做时间提醒（"还剩 15 分钟，这个话题还要继续吗？"）。

• Be ready to reschedule if needed.
• 必要时干脆改期。
Meeting feels dead
会议死气沉沉		• No one is engaged, and ideas stall.
• 没人投入，想法停滞。

• Time wasted as the meeting is going nowhere.
• 会议毫无进展，白白浪费时间。		• Pause and reassess if the meeting should continue.
• 暂停一下，重新评估这场会是否还要继续。

• Diagnose root causes: low energy, unclear purpose, lack of safety?
• 诊断根因：是士气低落？目的不清？还是缺少安全感？

• Adapt the format or split into smaller problems.
• 调整形式，或把问题拆小。
Meetings turn into fights
会议变成争吵		• Kills trust.
• 扼杀信任。

• Derails teamwork.
• 破坏协作。

• Decision making breaks down.
• 决策无法推进。		• Bring people back to the problem you are trying to solve.
• 把大家拉回到要解决的问题上。

• Shift from "me versus you" to "us versus the problem." Find common ground early.
• 从"你我对立"转向"我们共同面对问题"。尽早找到共同点。

• Ask for clarification openly: "Can you explain that again?"
• 公开地请对方澄清："你能再解释一遍吗？"
No clear outcome at the end
结束时没有明确结论		• Participants leave confused.
• 与会者一头雾水地离开。

• No clear next steps so nothing happens.
• 没有明确的后续步骤，于是什么也没发生。		• Assign a note-taker other than you as facilitator.
• 安排一个记录员，而不是由主持人自己兼任。

• Summarize what was discussed and what was agreed on, and assign next steps and owners. Validate assumptions live: "If I understand correctly, you mean X."
• 总结讨论了什么、达成了什么一致，并明确后续步骤和负责人。当场验证理解："如果我理解得没错，你的意思是 X。"

• Write final agreements on a shared document live during the meeting.
• 会议进行中就把最终共识实时写进共享文档。
Nothing happens after the meeting
会后毫无动静		• Wasted time discussing.
• 讨论的时间白费了。

• Erodes trust.
• 侵蚀信任。		Have a clear process for following up: e.g., a quick follow-up message to the action owners, a shared doc to track progress, or a check-in meeting if needed.
建立清晰的跟进流程：例如给行动负责人发一条简短的跟进消息、用共享文档追踪进展，必要时再开一次检查会。
— PDF p.292 —

To run effective decision-making meetings, you need more than a calendar invite. Here are some concrete steps to help you create structure, keep discussions focused, and ensure clear outcomes:

要开好高效的决策会议，光有日历邀请是不够的。下面是一些具体步骤，帮你建立结构、让讨论聚焦，并确保结论清晰：

— PDF p.293 —

Set up a clear goal and structure. Before the meeting, ask yourself: if there’s just one thing I want to achieve by the end of this meeting, what would it be? Not five things, just one.

设定清晰的目标与结构。开会前先问自己：如果这场会结束时我只想达成一件事，那会是什么？不是五件，就一件。

Define it clearly in the meeting invite title and description. Add links to previous discussions or draft plans if they exist. When the meeting starts, restate the goal clearly and walk through a brief agenda, setting expectations for how the time will be used.

把它清晰地写进会议邀请的标题和描述里。如果有此前的讨论或草案计划，附上链接。会议开始时，清楚地重述目标，并过一遍简短议程，让大家对时间如何使用形成预期。

During the meeting, keep that goal top of mind. Whenever conversations start drifting, gently anchor people back by asking: "Is this relevant for the conversation?" or "How is this helping us reach our goal?"

会议进行中，把这个目标牢记在心。每当讨论开始跑偏，就温和地把大家锚定回来，问一句："这和当前讨论相关吗？"或"这对我们达成目标有什么帮助？"

Sometimes, the realization hits that the original goal of the meeting no longer makes sense. For example, maybe the discussion was built on a flawed assumption or misalignment. In that case, don’t be afraid to abandon the original agenda and shift gears. Just make clear the new goal you will work toward. Letting the group flow toward what really needs to be addressed can be the most productive outcome.

有时你会意识到：这场会原本的目标已经不成立了。比如，讨论建立在一个错误的假设或不对齐之上。这时别怕放弃原议程、调转方向。只要讲清楚你们接下来要朝哪个新目标努力就行。让小组顺势去解决真正需要解决的问题，可能才是最有成效的结果。

Define and timebox the meeting structure. Set expectations up front on how much time you will spend on gathering ideas, discussing options, and making a decision.

定义会议结构并为其设定时间盒（timebox）。事先讲清楚：收集想法、讨论选项、做出决策，各花多少时间。

Assign a timekeeper. It can be you as the facilitator or someone else in the group. The timekeeper’s role is simple but important: keeping the pace and reminding the group when time is running out so you still have enough time to conclude properly.

指定一名计时员。可以是作为主持人的你，也可以是组里的其他人。计时员的角色简单但重要：把控节奏，在时间将尽时提醒大家，好让你还有足够时间好好收尾。

That said, sometimes things don’t go according to plan. If the decision needs more time, acknowledge it honestly. Summarize where you are, document the partial outcome, and propose a follow-up session.

话虽如此，有时事情不会按计划走。如果这个决策需要更多时间，就坦诚承认。总结你们目前进展到哪一步，记录下阶段性结论，并提议再开一次跟进会。

Use visual tools to ensure alignment. One of my favorite techniques is whiteboarding. Use a whiteboard or a digital tool like FigJam or Miro so that everyone can contribute ideas, see what’s being discussed, and track progress live. Visual tools help people process complex topics better and spot gaps or misalignments faster.

用可视化工具确保对齐。我最喜欢的技巧之一就是画白板。用一块白板，或 FigJam、Miro 之类的数字工具，让每个人都能贡献想法、看到正在讨论什么、并实时追踪进展。可视化工具能帮助人们更好地处理复杂话题，更快地发现缺口或不对齐之处。

Another great tool is a RAID board, where you track risks, assumptions, issues, and dependencies.

另一个很好用的工具是 RAID 看板，用来追踪风险（risks）、假设（assumptions）、问题（issues）和依赖（dependencies）。

Also, having a dedicated space to park side conversations or concerns (like a "Parking Lot" board) ensures people feel heard without derailing the main conversation.

此外，专门辟一个地方（比如一块"停车场"看板）来暂存题外话或顾虑，能让大家觉得自己被听到，又不会让主讨论跑偏。

— PDF p.294 —

Use different tools to capture ideas. Not everyone feels comfortable sharing ideas out loud. Some people might prefer writing them down.

用不同的工具来捕捉想法。并非每个人都习惯大声说出自己的想法，有些人可能更愿意写下来。

So use multiple channels for input: anonymous forms, one-on-one discussions, or Post-it notes.

因此要用多种渠道收集意见：匿名表单、一对一沟通，或者便利贴。

Separating the idea from the person makes it easier to have objective, less heated conversations around options and trade-offs. This creates a safer space for honest debate.

把"想法"和"提出想法的人"分离开，更容易围绕选项和权衡进行客观、少带情绪的讨论。这为坦诚的辩论创造了更安全的空间。

Constantly validate assumptions. Most misalignments happen because people think they are on the same page when they are not.

不断验证假设。大多数不对齐，都发生在"人们以为大家步调一致、其实并非如此"的时候。

Make it a habit to regularly validate what you hear. Use simple phrases like "If I understand correctly, you mean…" to clarify.

养成习惯，经常验证你听到的内容。用"如果我理解得没错，你的意思是……"这样简单的话来澄清。

It might feel repetitive, but catching misunderstandings early is always better than cleaning up miscommunications later.

这可能显得重复，但及早发现误解，永远好过事后再来收拾沟通失误的烂摊子。

Make agreements specific and document them. Before ending any meeting, take a moment to spell out the decisions made.

让共识具体化并记录下来。结束任何会议之前，花一点时间把做出的决策逐条讲清楚。

I always say it out loud: "Ana will work on X. John will review Y."

我总会大声念出来："Ana 负责做 X，John 负责评审 Y。"

I immediately write it down live in a shared document while sharing my screen with the group. This turns the meeting into a visible, living commitment. No more "I thought you meant…" conversations afterward. And funnily enough, very often someone will chime in at this point: "Wait, that’s not what I understood." Exactly what you want to uncover before leaving the room.

我会一边给大家共享屏幕，一边当场把它写进共享文档。这让会议变成一个看得见、活生生的承诺。之后就不会再有"我以为你的意思是……"的扯皮了。而且很有意思的是，往往就在这时有人会插话："等等，我理解的不是这样。"——而这恰恰就是你在离开会议室之前想挖出来的东西。

Follow up. Without proper follow-up, even the best meetings turn into wasted time.

跟进。没有恰当的跟进，再好的会议也会变成浪费时间。

Always define the next step: maybe it’s setting up a follow-up meeting; maybe it’s agreeing when progress will be reviewed asynchronously.

永远要定义下一步：也许是安排一次跟进会，也许是约定何时异步地检查进展。

Whatever it is, make it clear how and when the actions will be revisited. Otherwise, things get lost in the chaos of daily work.

不管是什么，都要讲清楚这些行动将在何时、以何种方式被重新检视。否则，事情就会淹没在日常工作的混乱之中。

Beyond structure and logistics, facilitation is also about navigating group dynamics, energy, and communication. These extra techniques will help you lead smoother, more inclusive, and more productive decision-making sessions:

除了结构和流程安排之外，主持还关乎驾驭群体动力、团队士气和沟通。下面这些额外技巧，会帮你主持出更顺畅、更包容、更有成效的决策会议：

— PDF p.295 —

Facilitation starts before (and continues after) the meeting. Sometimes, especially for complex topics, you’ll need to help people show up ready. That might mean priming them with questions to think about in advance, reminding them to do the reading, or even summarizing key points in advance if you know your team doesn’t always prepare.

主持在会议之前就开始（并在会议之后延续）。有时，尤其是面对复杂话题，你需要帮助大家"带着准备"来开会。这可能意味着提前抛给他们一些思考题、提醒他们去读材料，甚至——如果你知道团队不总会提前准备——提前把要点总结好。

If half the attendees show up unprepared, you’ll have to decide whether to adapt in the moment, perhaps by spending time reviewing the materials together or rescheduling with clearer guidance.

如果一半与会者都没准备，你就得决定：是临场调整（比如花时间一起过一遍材料），还是带着更明确的指引改期。

Prioritize "moving forward together" over "being right." Don’t just focus on proving your solution is the best! In fact, if you can’t get others on board, it might be a sign your solution needs rethinking.

把"共同前进"置于"证明自己正确"之上。别一门心思只想证明你的方案最好！事实上，如果你无法让其他人认同，那可能恰恰说明你的方案需要重新思考。

What matters most is finding a path the whole team is willing to commit to. Alignment doesn’t mean everyone agrees 100%, but it does mean there’s shared ownership and a collective commitment to move forward together.

最重要的是找到一条整个团队都愿意投入的路。对齐并不意味着每个人都 100% 同意，但它确实意味着：大家共同拥有这条路，并共同承诺一起往前走。

Consistency is often more valuable than the "correct" technical choice. If it’s not an approach we absolutely want to move away from—because it’s clearly outdated or fundamentally flawed—then sticking with what we used last time is often the better choice. This applies the most when we are talking about technical tools, although the rule applies more generally as well. Consistency reduces cognitive load, and having clear, consistent ways of doing things matters far more than chasing trends or perfect solutions.

一致性，往往比"正确"的技术选择更有价值。只要不是那种我们明确想摆脱的做法——因为它显然过时或存在根本缺陷——那么沿用上次的做法通常就是更好的选择。这条在谈到技术工具时尤其适用，不过它在更广范围内也成立。一致性能降低认知负担；拥有清晰、一贯的做事方式，远比追逐潮流或追求完美方案重要。

It doesn’t always have to be you facilitating. It actually makes your job way harder to be the tech lead, the facilitator, the developer, and the team member in the same meeting. Once things are running smoothly, I suggest training others in facilitation skills. It’s a great growth opportunity for them and frees you up to contribute better during meetings.

主持不必总是你一个人来。在同一场会上同时扮演技术负责人、主持人、开发者和普通团队成员，实际上会让你的工作难上加难。一旦运转顺畅，我建议去培养其他人的主持能力。这对他们是很好的成长机会，也能把你解放出来，在会上贡献更好的想法。

With facilitation comes power, not just responsibility. People often forget that the role of facilitator doesn’t just come with responsibility; it comes with power. The power to shape the flow of the conversation, to make space for quieter voices, to steer the group back when things go off track. It’s subtle, but it’s real.

主持带来的不仅是责任，还有权力。人们常常忘记：主持人这个角色伴随的不只是责任，还有权力——塑造讨论走向、为安静的声音留出空间、在跑偏时把小组拉回来的权力。它很微妙，但真实存在。

And if you’re stepping into the role of facilitator, especially as a tech lead, it’s important that you use that power thoughtfully.

而当你走上主持人这个岗位、尤其是作为技术负责人时，重要的是要审慎地使用这份权力。

— PDF p.296 —

Use it to balance participation by asking people to raise their hands before speaking. This allows you to guide the conversation and ensure space for quieter voices, not just the most vocal.

用它来平衡参与度：请大家发言前先举手。这样你就能引导对话，确保给安静的人留出空间，而不只是让最能说的人说了算。

Use it to create space for quieter voices, with prompts like "Would anyone like to offer a different perspective?" You can also gently invite someone directly—"July, what do you think?"—as long as you’ve checked beforehand that they’re comfortable being called on.

用它为安静的声音创造空间，比如提示一句："有没有人想提供一个不同的视角？"你也可以温和地直接邀请某人——"July，你怎么看？"——前提是你事先确认过对方不介意被点名。

If a conversation is getting too heated and going nowhere, don’t be afraid to break the tension: "OK, pause! I see we all care deeply about this. How could we move forward from here?"

如果一场讨论变得过于激烈、又毫无进展，别害怕打破紧张气氛："好，暂停一下！我看得出大家都非常在乎这件事。我们怎么才能从这里往前走？"

Use your facilitator role to keep momentum when a discussion starts drifting. If a new topic comes up that’s not urgent but still valuable, you can say, "I see this is not something we can address right now, but it’s a risk worth capturing. Maybe we can just add it on our RAID board for now and return to our main point?"

当讨论开始跑偏时，用主持人的角色保持势头。如果冒出一个不紧急但有价值的新话题，你可以说："我看这件事现在没法处理，但它是个值得记录的风险。要不我们先把它记到 RAID 看板上，然后回到正题？"

And when things go completely off course, don’t hesitate to bring the group back with a simple "I feel we’re derailing a bit here. Let’s recap what we already discussed."

而当事情彻底跑偏时，别犹豫，用一句简单的话把小组拉回来："我感觉我们有点跑题了，咱们回顾一下已经讨论过的内容吧。"

Manage team energy, not just time. In longer sessions or recurring meetings, your team’s energy becomes just as important as the agenda. Fatigue leads to disengagement, rushed decisions, or conversations dominated by a few voices.

管理团队的士气，而不只是时间。在较长的会议或周期性会议中，团队的精力和议程一样重要。疲惫会导致 disengaged（投入度下降）、决策仓促，或讨论被少数声音主导。

Be mindful of how people are doing. Plan for breaks. If you’re in person, energizers and movement-based activities can help reset focus.

留心大家的状态。安排休息。如果是面对面，一些暖场小游戏和动一动的活动，能帮助重新集中注意力。

Even small gestures can set the tone. For example, I used to bring coffee and croissants for my team every time I got the chance during our sprint planning. It was an early morning meeting every two weeks, and this small routine helped start things on a positive, relaxed note.

哪怕是小小的举动，也能定下基调。比如，我以前每次做 sprint 规划时，只要有机会就会给团队带咖啡和可颂面包。那是每两周一次的早会，这个小小的习惯帮助大家以积极、放松的状态开场。

The format matters too: switching from group discussion to silent writing or pairing exercises can refresh the team and maintain engagement.

形式也很重要：从小组讨论切换到静默书写或结对练习，能让团队重新焕发生机、保持投入。

The best ideas often come when people are relaxed and recharged.

最好的点子，往往诞生在人们放松、充满电的时候。

— PDF p.297 —

Facilitating technical decisions well is one of the most useful and underrated skills of a tech lead. It’s about creating the space where the best solutions can emerge and making sure your team is aligned enough to act on them.

把技术决策主持好，是技术负责人最有用、却也最被低估的技能之一。它关乎创造一个空间，让最好的解决方案得以浮现，并确保团队对齐到足以据此行动。

Track Technical Decisions—Architecture Decision Records追踪技术决策——架构决策记录（ADR）

All the technical decisions you are making as a team should be tracked and made visible, to your current team and to any future team members who’ll wonder "Why did we do it this way?" You want a record that captures how the decision was made, what trade-offs were considered, and what consequences were accepted.

你们作为团队做出的所有技术决策，都应当被追踪、被看见——既给当前的团队看，也给将来会疑惑"我们当时为什么这么做"的新成员看。你需要一份记录，捕捉决策是如何做出的、考虑了哪些权衡、以及接受了哪些后果。

This is where architecture decision records (ADRs) come in.

这正是架构决策记录（architecture decision records，ADR）派上用场的地方。

ADRs are a lightweight and effective way to capture the team’s understanding at a specific point in time. They reflect the best decision made given the information available, along with the trade-offs considered. Instead of aiming for permanence, ADRs focus on documenting the context and reasoning behind a choice, so your future self, or others, don’t have to guess why something was done.

ADR 是一种轻量而有效的方式，用来捕捉团队在某个时间点上的理解。它反映的是：在当时可得信息下做出的最佳决策，以及所考虑的权衡。ADR 并不追求永恒不变，而是着重记录一个选择背后的来龙去脉和推理过程，好让未来的你或其他人，不必去猜当时为什么那么做。

Starting with ADRs从 ADR 开始

Start simple. The best way to begin using ADRs is by writing one for your next significant technical decision. Or even better, start by documenting a recent decision that’s already been made. This shifts the focus to learning the process rather than trying to capture everything perfectly in the moment.

从简单开始。开始使用 ADR 最好的方式，就是为你的下一个重要技术决策写一份。或者更好的做法是：先记录一个最近已经做出的决策。这会把重心放在学习流程上，而不是试图在当下把一切完美地捕捉下来。

Don’t overengineer it. Keep them lightweight and make it a habit. Encourage the team to use them anytime you’re facing a decision that’s architecturally significant, even if it feels small at the moment.

别把它过度工程化。保持轻量，并把它变成习惯。鼓励团队：每当面对一个在架构上有分量的决策时就用它记录下来，哪怕当时觉得它很小。

A simple ADR format might look like Table 9-3.

一个简单的 ADR 格式如表 9-3 所示。

One way to make this process stick is to integrate ADRs into your workflow. For example, make writing an ADR part of the definition of done for certain stories. When a story includes a technical decision, require the team to capture it in an ADR before it’s considered complete. This way, the habit becomes part of how you build.

让这个流程扎根的一个办法，是把 ADR 集成到你的工作流里。例如，把"写一份 ADR"作为某些用户故事完成标准（definition of done）的一部分。当一个故事包含技术决策时，要求团队在它被视为完成之前，先把决策记录进 ADR。这样，这个习惯就成了你构建方式的一部分。

— PDF p.298 —

Table 9-3. Simple ADR format.

表 9-3. 简单的 ADR 格式。

# ADR title
Give it a clear, descriptive name. Match the file name so it's easy to search.

## Context
Describe what you knew at the time:
What constraints were you working under? Or: What challenges were you solving?
Stay neutral: just the facts.
List any alternatives that were explored and why they were rejected.

## Decision
Clearly state what you decided. Use full sentences, in an active voice: "We will..."

## Consequences
Spell out what this means, both good and bad. For example:
  - This introduces tech debt we'll address post-launch.
  - This approach supports X but makes Y more difficult.
  - Although option Z was preferred by some, we agreed to go with this and revisit later.
Capturing consequences is often the most valuable part. It shows the trade-offs.
It creates alignment. And it gives your future self a realistic picture of what you
signed up for.

---
Extra information
e.g., Date, Status, Related ADRs, ...

Use ADRs as a tool during conversations. Capture options discussed, trade-offs considered, and concerns raised while the decision is being made, not just after it’s done.

把 ADR 当作对话中的工具来用。在决策正在形成的过程中，就把讨论过的选项、权衡过的取舍、提出过的顾虑都记录下来，而不只是在决策做完之后。

Example of an ADRADR 示例

You can see how a simple ADR might look in practice in Table 9-4. This example shows how to capture the context, the decision, and the consequences in a lightweight format that’s easy to read, share, and update. The goal is to create a shared understanding your team can refer back to.

表 9-4 展示了一个简单的 ADR 在实践中大概是什么样子。这个例子展示了如何用一种轻量、易读、易分享、易更新的格式，来记录背景、决策和后果。目标是创造一种共享的理解，让团队日后可以随时回查。

— PDF p.299 —

Table 9-4. Example of an ADR (file: adr-0001-use-postgresql-as-main-database.md).

表 9-4. ADR 示例（文件名：adr-0001-use-postgresql-as-main-database.md）。

# ADR-0001: Use PostgreSQL

## Context
We need a reliable, open source relational database that works well with our tech stack
(Node.js + TypeScript).
The product roadmap involves features that require strong consistency guarantees,
transactional support, and a flexible schema.

Options considered:
PostgreSQL: Strong match for our needs. Already used in other services. Team has
  solid experience. Rich ecosystem and tooling.
MySQL: Similar to PostgreSQL but lacks some advanced features we may rely on
  (e.g., JSONB support).
MongoDB: Flexible and fast to prototype with but lacks the consistency guarantees and
  transactional support needed for billing-related features.
DynamoDB: Highly scalable but has a restrictive query model and would require a
  significant shift in tooling and team expertise.

## Decision
We will use PostgreSQL as our primary database for the new billing service.

## Consequences
[+] Alignment with team skill set and existing infrastructure.
[+] Strong ecosystem and tooling support.
[-] Higher operational complexity than DynamoDB.
[-] Less flexible for schema-less data, which we'll address with JSONB columns
  where needed.
[+] Easy integration with our current CI/CD pipeline and monitoring stack.

Note: Option Z (MongoDB) had some strong internal support, but we agreed to revisit
if needs change.

---
Date: 2025-04-28
Status: Accepted
Supersedes: None
Related ADRs: None
— PDF p.300 —

ADRs challengesADR 的常见挑战

There are several challenges you’re likely to encounter when it comes to ADRs. Here they are:

在使用 ADR 时，你很可能会遇到下面几个挑战。

Storing ADRsADR 存放在哪里

Tech teams often debate whether to store ADRs in a single shared repo, spread them across individual services, or place them in tools like Notion or Confluence. The key is context: what problem are you solving?

技术团队经常争论：ADR 到底该放在一个共享仓库里、分散在各个服务中，还是放在 Notion 或 Confluence 这类工具里。关键在于语境：你要解决的是什么问题？

A good starting point is to keep ADRs local to the service where the decision applies, in the same repository as the code. This makes them easy to find, keeps them versioned alongside the implementation, and allows your team to use the same tools for editing.

一个不错的起点是：把 ADR 放在决策所适用的那个服务本地，与代码放在同一个仓库里。这样它们容易被找到、与实现一起被版本管理，团队也能用同一套工具来编辑。

Over time, you might find it useful to move some ADRs to a centralized repo, especially if they apply to multiple teams, you’re standardizing practices across the org, or tooling makes service-level storage less practical. This shift often happens when architectural guidance needs to be shared more broadly or when your company has specific guidelines for ADR storage.

随着时间推移，你可能会发现把某些 ADR 挪到一个集中仓库里更有用——尤其是当它们适用于多个团队、你在全组织范围内统一做法，或者工具使得按服务存放不那么现实的时候。这种转变通常发生在：架构指引需要被更广泛地分享，或者公司对 ADR 存放有专门规定时。

Any approach works, as long as your team knows where to find them and follows a consistent process.

任何方式都行，只要你的团队知道去哪里找，并且遵循一致的流程。

But what matters most isn’t where you store ADRs; it’s that you actually write them and make them accessible. Don’t let the storage debate drain your team energy. Pick something and move forward. You can always move them later. At the end of the day, it’s just text.

但最重要的不是你把 ADR 存在哪里，而是你真的去写、并且让它们容易被查阅。别让"存哪儿"的争论耗尽团队精力。选一个，往前走。以后随时可以再挪。说到底，它不过就是文本。

— PDF p.301 —

Updating ADRs如何更新 ADR

Keeping ADRs in the same repo as the code also makes it easy to update them. There are two common styles here: some teams update the original ADR file and use Git versioning to track changes. Others prefer to create a new ADR entirely and mark the old one as deprecated or superseded.

把 ADR 和代码放在同一个仓库里，也让更新变得容易。这里有两种常见做法：有些团队直接更新原 ADR 文件，并用 Git 的版本管理来追踪变更；另一些团队则倾向于另写一份全新的 ADR，并把旧的标记为"已废弃"或"已被取代"。

Either approach is fine; the key is clarity. If you’re writing a new ADR to replace an old one, make sure to add a note in the original: "This decision has been superseded by [ADR-0023-NewTitle]." That way, future readers won’t be left wondering which guidance to follow.

两种做法都可以，关键是清晰。如果你是在写一份新的 ADR 来取代旧的，务必在旧文件里加一句说明："本决策已被 [ADR-0023-NewTitle] 取代。"这样，未来的读者就不会困惑该遵循哪一份。

When deciding which approach to take, consider your audience. If your ADRs are read by people outside the engineering team, like product managers or business analysts, it may be better to create a new ADR and deprecate the old one. That way, the full reasoning behind each change is clearly visible and easy to understand without having to dig through Git history.

在决定用哪种做法时，考虑你的读者。如果你的 ADR 会被工程团队之外的人读到——比如产品经理或业务分析师——那么新建一份 ADR、把旧的废弃掉可能更好。这样，每次变更背后的完整推理都清晰可见、容易理解，不必去翻 Git 历史。

On the other hand, if your readers are comfortable with Git and prefer a compact history, updating the existing file might be the cleaner option. Pick the approach that makes decisions easy to trace for your team.

反之，如果你的读者熟悉 Git、更喜欢紧凑的历史记录，那么直接更新现有文件可能更干净。选那个让团队容易追溯决策的做法。

What counts as “architecturally significant”?什么才算“在架构上有分量”？

Another challenge is knowing what’s worth documenting. Don’t write an ADR for every small config tweak. Focus on architecturally significant decisions: things that shape how you work, structure your codebase, handle failure, or scale. Things like how you handle authentication, which database to use, changing from REST to GraphQL, how you approach retries and timeouts, or where you draw service boundaries.

另一个挑战是判断什么值得记录。别为每一个小小的配置改动都写 ADR。聚焦于在架构上有分量的决策：那些塑造你工作方式、代码库结构、故障处理或扩展性的事情。比如：如何处理认证、用哪个数据库、从 REST 改为 GraphQL、如何处理重试与超时，或者服务边界划在哪里。

If you’re unsure, ask: "Would someone new on the team benefit from knowing why we chose this approach?"

如果你拿不准，就问自己一句："团队新来的人，会因为知道我们当初为什么选这个做法而受益吗？"

Who owns ADRs?ADR 由谁负责？

Ideally, ownership is shared across the team. But, as always, when everyone is responsible, no one is, so it helps to clarify who’s responsible for maintaining ADRs, whether it’s the person driving the decision or a rotating role. Don’t let ADRs become stale just because no one feels accountable.

理想情况下，ADR 的所有权由团队共享。但老话总不错：当人人都负责时，就没人负责了。所以最好明确谁来维护 ADR——是推动这个决策的人，还是一个轮值的角色。别让 ADR 因为没人觉得该自己负责而变得过时。

Besides documenting decisions, ADRs also act as a kind of contract, a shared commitment from the team to follow a chosen path, knowing the trade-offs. They help you move forward even when there’s disagreement, by acknowledging concerns and leaving space to revisit them later.

除了记录决策之外，ADR 还扮演着一种契约的角色——团队在明知权衡的情况下，对走上某条路所做的共同承诺。通过承认顾虑、并留出日后重新检视的空间，ADR 帮助你们即便存在分歧也能继续前进。

For example, imagine two developers arguing over which JSON library to use. If the team already made a decision months ago and documented it in an ADR, with the options considered, trade-offs, and rationale, it can help settle the discussion quickly. Of course, if new context emerges, you can revisit the decision. But in many cases, it saves time and prevents rehashing debates over choices that were already made thoughtfully.

举个例子，想象两个开发者在争该用哪个 JSON 库。如果团队几个月前就做过决策、并写进了 ADR——连同考虑过的选项、权衡和理由——它就能帮你迅速平息争论。当然，如果出现了新的语境，你可以重新检视这个决策。但在很多情况下，它节省了时间，避免了把已经深思熟虑过的选择又拿出来反复争论。

Used well, ADRs are a low-effort, high-impact way to preserve team knowledge, align on decisions, and reduce friction as your product and team evolve. Especially in fast-moving environments, they’re one of the simplest ways to protect your team’s context, and one of the easiest habits to adopt that pays off in the long run.

用得好的话，ADR 是一种低成本、高回报的方式，用来保存团队知识、在决策上对齐，并在产品和团队演进时减少摩擦。尤其在快节奏的环境里，它们是保护团队上下文最简单的方式之一，也是最容易养成、并能长期带来回报的习惯之一。

— PDF p.302 —

Encouraging Technical Excellence鼓励技术卓越

Technical excellence doesn’t just happen. It’s the result of shared, intentional decisions, how we build, how we review, how we test, and how we operate. As a tech lead, your role is to create the environment where those decisions are made deliberately and consistently.

技术卓越不会凭空发生。它是一系列共享的、有意识的决策的结果——我们如何构建、如何评审、如何测试、如何运维。作为技术负责人，你的角色是创造一个环境，让这些决策被审慎而一贯地做出。

Your job is to keep the bar high by making it visible, agreed upon, and reflected in how your team actually works. That means setting clear expectations, building strong engineering habits, and reinforcing the idea that quality is a shared responsibility.

你的工作是把标准维持在高位——让它看得见、被大家认同，并体现在团队真实的工作方式中。这意味着设定清晰的预期、建立扎实的工程习惯，并不断强化"质量是大家共同的责任"这一观念。

In this section, you’ll learn how to define standards that feel shared and meaningful, ones your team actively commits to, instead of rules handed down from above.

在本节中，你会学到如何定义那些让人觉得是"共享的、有意义的"标准——团队会主动投入去遵守的标准，而不是自上而下压下来的规则。

I’ll also cover how to build fast feedback loops through integration and deployment, how to use measurement to guide thoughtful improvement, and how to make testing a consistent and valuable part of everyday development work.

我还会讲到：如何通过集成与部署构建快速反馈回路、如何用度量来引导深思熟虑的改进，以及如何让测试成为日常开发中一贯而有价值的一部分。

Define Team Standards定义团队标准

As a tech lead, you play a key role in helping your team align on what “good” looks like, technically and operationally, as well as behaviorally.

作为技术负责人，你在帮助团队就"好是什么样"达成对齐方面扮演着关键角色——无论是技术上、运维上，还是行为方式上。

You may already have company-wide guidelines or platform-level constraints, but within your team, you still need to define your own local standards. These are the agreements that help your team move fast together, without reinventing the wheel for every decision.

公司层面的指引或平台层面的约束或许已经存在，但在你的团队内部，你仍然需要定义自己的本地标准。这些约定帮助团队协同快速前进，而不必为每个决策都重新发明轮子。

When we say “standards,” we don’t just mean linting rules or test coverage thresholds. We’re talking about agreements at every level of how your team operates:

当我们说"标准"时，指的不只是 lint 规则或测试覆盖率阈值。我们说的是团队运作方方面面的约定：

  • How decisions are made (see the section "Help Your Team Make Technical Decisions" on page 272)决策如何做出（参见第 272 页"帮助团队做出技术决策"一节）
  • How the system evolves (see the section "Build a Technical Vision (and Turn It into a Strategy)" on page 269 and the section "Track Technical Decisions—Architecture Decision Records" on page 281)系统如何演进（参见第 269 页"构建技术愿景（并转化为战略）"和第 281 页"追踪技术决策——架构决策记录"两节）
  • How code gets written, reviewed, and shipped (see the section "Aim for Fast Feedback" on page 287 and the section "Ensure Quality Through Testing" on page 290)代码如何编写、评审和发布（参见第 287 页"追求快速反馈"和第 290 页"通过测试保障质量"两节）
— PDF p.303 —
  • How priorities are chosen and delivery is tracked (see the section "Planning and Keeping a Project on Track" on page 291 and the section "Balancing Multiple Streams of Work" on page 297)优先级如何确定、交付如何追踪（参见第 291 页"规划并让项目不脱轨"和第 297 页"平衡多条工作流"两节）
  • How you work together as a team (see the section "How to Build a Healthy Team Culture" on page 185)你们作为一个团队如何协作（参见第 185 页"如何打造健康的团队文化"一节）

These agreements form the invisible scaffolding of your day-to-day work. When they’re unclear or inconsistent, the team slows down. People second-guess what “done” means. Decisions take longer. Reviews are frustrating. Quality drops.

这些约定构成了你日常工作中看不见的脚手架。当它们模糊或不一致时，团队就会慢下来。人们会反复琢磨"完成"到底意味着什么。决策更耗时。评审令人沮丧。质量下滑。

But when your standards are clear and shared, your team can work independently without diverging. You don’t have to be in every conversation or review every line of code. Because the expectations are understood, decisions can scale.

而当你的标准清晰、被大家共享时，团队就能独立工作而不偏离方向。你不必参与每一场讨论，也不必评审每一行代码。因为预期是被理解的，决策就可以规模化地推进。

As a tech lead, don’t define these standards alone; create space for the team to define them together. That might mean running a workshop, reflecting in a retrospective, or revisiting old documentation that no longer reflects reality. It’s less about writing rules and more about surfacing assumptions and creating alignment.

作为技术负责人，别独自定义这些标准；要创造空间让团队一起定义。这可能意味着办一场工作坊、在回顾会上反思，或者重新审视那些已不再反映现实的旧文档。重点不在于写规则，而在于把假设摆上台面、创造对齐。

One trap to watch out for: having overly aspirational standards that no one actually follows. A great rule of thumb is this: your standards should reflect what you’re willing to review and uphold, not just what you hope for. They should be visible, actionable, and revisited regularly, especially as the team changes or the product evolves.

要警惕一个陷阱：定了过于理想化、却没人真正遵守的标准。一个很好的经验法则是：你的标准应当反映你愿意去评审、去维护的东西，而不只是你希望的东西。它们应当看得见、可执行，并被定期重新检视——尤其是在团队变动或产品演进时。

You don’t need to solve every disagreement up front. But do agree on a mechanism for resolving them. Standards evolve, and that’s healthy. What matters is that your team knows where to look, how to propose a change, and how to hold each other accountable.

你不必一开始就解决每一个分歧。但要就"如何解决分歧"达成一个机制。标准会演进，这是健康的。重要的是你的团队知道去哪里查、如何提出变更、以及如何互相督促。

Aim for Fast Feedback追求快速反馈

In Chapter 8, I talked about the value of having great processes for continuously delivering high-quality value to your customers, and shipping code that’s been tested, validated, and is up to standard.

在第 8 章里，我谈到了拥有良好流程的价值——持续地把高质量的价值交付给客户，并发布经过测试、验证、达标的代码。

But even with the best processes, things will go wrong. That’s inevitable. And the only way to know when they go wrong, and how fast you can react, is by having the right observability in place. Metrics, alerts, and alarms are your early warning system. Without them, you’re flying blind and will discover issues only once they’ve already impacted users.

但即便是最好的流程，也会出问题。这是不可避免的。而要知道何时出了问题、以及你能多快反应，唯一的办法就是拥有恰当的可观测性。指标、告警和警报就是你的预警系统。没有它们，你就是在盲人摸象，只能在问题已经影响到用户之后才发现。

— PDF p.304 —

As a tech lead, you’re not expected to be an observability expert, but you are expected to care—making sure the right signals are in place and that people are paying attention to them. You’re responsible for asking the right questions: Do we actually know when something’s broken? Are we measuring what matters? Can the team respond quickly when things go wrong?

作为技术负责人，你不必是可观测性专家，但你被期待去关心它——确保恰当的信号到位，并且有人在关注这些信号。你有责任问出正确的问题：我们真的能在东西坏了的时候知道吗？我们度量的是真正重要的东西吗？出问题时团队能快速响应吗？

Your role is to guide the conversation. Help your team align on what “good enough” observability looks like. Push for clarity over coverage. Facilitate decisions about what to monitor, what can be dropped, and how to stay on top of what matters as your system evolves. Think of yourself as the person connecting the dots: from business impact to system behavior, from vague symptoms to root causes, and from noisy signals to actionable alerts.

你的角色是引导对话。帮助团队就"足够好的可观测性是什么样"达成对齐。推动"清晰"优先于"覆盖"。主持决策：监控什么、可以丢弃什么、以及随着系统演进如何始终掌握真正重要的东西。把自己想象成那个"把点连起来"的人：从业务影响连到系统行为，从模糊症状连到根因，从嘈杂信号连到可行动的告警。

The first issue I’ve seen with observability is the most obvious one: no data. Just not enough visibility into what’s happening in your system to make any useful decisions.

我见过的可观测性第一个问题，也是最明显的一个：没有数据。对系统里正在发生的事情可见度太低，根本没法做出有用的决策。

But more often, the bigger problem isn’t too little data; it’s too much. Any observability tool you hook up to your services will come with dozens of automatic metrics. Suddenly you’ve got too many dashboards, too many graphs, and too many alerts, many of them noisy, low-value, and constantly blinking yellow. You stop trusting them. You ignore them. And when something really does go wrong, it’s hard to see the signal through all the noise.

但更常见的情况是，更大的问题不是数据太少，而是数据太多。你接到服务上的任何可观测性工具，都会自带几十项自动指标。突然之间，你有了太多仪表盘、太多图表、太多告警，其中许多又吵又没用、还老闪黄灯。你开始不信任它们。你开始无视它们。而当真的出问题时，你很难在一片噪音里看清信号。

This happens because teams treat observability like a side task, something separate from product work. Someone adds a few metrics “just in case.” Another person adds some alerts without checking if they’re actually useful. Rarely do we go back and clean things up. Rarely do we ask: is this data still helping us?

这种情况的发生，是因为团队把可观测性当成了一个旁支任务、一件与产品工作分开的事。某个人"以防万一"地加了几个指标。另一个人没去核实有没有用就加了些告警。我们很少回头去清理。很少去问：这些数据现在还在帮我们吗？

As a tech lead responsible for a product, I basically want to know two things: is it available? and does it work as expected?

作为一个对产品负责的技术负责人，我基本上只想知道两件事：它可用吗？它按预期工作吗？

I remember a time when our dashboards were filled with charts no one could explain. We had alerts firing at random times, most of which we ignored. Then one weekend, something actually broke, and it took us hours to realize it because the real issue was buried under noise. That was the moment I realized we needed fewer, more meaningful signals, metrics that actually meant something to us.

我记得有一次，我们的仪表盘上塞满了没人能解释的图表。我们的告警在随机时间响，大多数都被我们无视了。后来有个周末，真的出故障了，我们花了好几个小时才发现——因为真正的问题被埋在噪音底下。那一刻我意识到：我们需要更少、但更有意义的信号，真正对我们有意义的指标。

If you’re dealing with observability noise, here’s my suggestion: start fresh. Forget your current dashboards for a second. Sit down with your team and ask, “What do we actually need to monitor? What’s a real problem? What are the alarms we would wake up in the middle of the night for?”

如果你正被可观测性的噪音困扰，我的建议是：重新开始。先把你现有的仪表盘忘掉。和团队坐下来问："我们到底需要监控什么？什么才算真正的问题？哪些警报是值得我们半夜爬起来去处理的？"

— PDF p.305 —

When your team defines what matters together, you create clarity around what “good” looks like, what constitutes a real issue, and where to focus during incidents. This shared understanding can dramatically reduce noise, speed up incident response, and build a stronger sense of ownership across the team.

当团队一起定义什么才重要时，你就对"好是什么样""什么算真正的问题""事故期间该聚焦哪里"形成了清晰的共识。这种共享的理解能大幅减少噪音、加快事故响应，并在团队中建立更强的主人翁感。

Start from there. A good rule of thumb: one dashboard per product, not per service. All the key metrics should fit on a single screen. If you glance at it and can’t immediately tell whether things are OK, something’s wrong. And the metrics need to be meaningful. Metrics aren’t useful unless they tell you when something is wrong.

从这里开始。一个好的经验法则：每个产品一块仪表盘，而不是每个服务一块。所有关键指标应当能放进一个屏幕。如果你扫一眼，没法立刻判断一切是否正常，那就有问题。而且指标要有意义。指标若不能告诉你"什么时候出了问题"，它就毫无用处。

This requires a mindset shift. Instead of asking “What should we measure?” ask “When is it actually a problem?” Define your service-level indicators and service-level objectives. Set limits. Tune/refine/iterate on thresholds. And be courageous enough to delete what doesn’t help. If you have an alert that’s always red but you never act on it, do you really care about it? Probably not.

这需要一次思维转变。别问"我们该度量什么"，而要问"什么时候它才算真的出问题"。定义你的服务等级指标（SLI）和服务等级目标（SLO）。设定界限。对阈值进行调优、打磨、迭代。并且要有勇气删掉没用的东西。如果你有一个告警老是响红、却从来没人去处理，你真的在乎它吗？大概并不。

Modern observability tools like Datadog and Grafana can often show you historical data, even for metrics you didn’t pre-configure, so don’t be afraid to remove noise. If you need something, you can add it back.

像 Datadog、Grafana 这样的现代可观测性工具，往往能展示历史数据——哪怕是你没有预先配置的指标。所以别害怕去删噪音。如果以后需要，再加回来就是。

Another strong habit: make observability part of your daily development work. Every feature, every task, should come with a conversation: “Do we need to monitor this? What does success or failure look like?” Add that to your definition of done.

另一个强有力的习惯：把可观测性变成你日常开发工作的一部分。每个功能、每个任务，都应伴随一场讨论："我们需要监控这个吗？成功或失败是什么样子？"把它加进你的完成标准里。

Good observability helps your team catch problems early and turn those problems into learning opportunities. When something breaks, a system with the right metrics and logs gives you clues about what happened, what went wrong, and why. This makes incident reviews more useful and less about finger-pointing. Over time, this turns incidents into learning opportunities. You start to see patterns, connect the dots, and use that insight to prevent future issues. That’s when observability becomes more than a safety net.

好的可观测性帮助团队及早发现问题，并把这些问题转化为学习的机会。当东西坏了时，一个拥有恰当指标和日志的系统会给你线索：发生了什么、哪里出了错、为什么。这让事故复盘更有价值、少一些互相指责。久而久之，事故就变成了学习机会。你开始看到模式、把点连起来，并用这种洞察去预防未来的问题。那时，可观测性就不再只是一张安全网了。

Observability is how your code talks back to you in production. If you can’t hear it clearly, you’re flying blind. Your goal isn’t more data; it’s faster feedback and better decisions.

可观测性，就是你的代码在生产环境里"回话"给你的方式。如果你听不清它，你就是在盲人摸象。你的目标不是更多数据，而是更快的反馈和更好的决策。

The tech lead plays a critical role in shaping observability culture. Your job is to make sure the right metrics and dashboards are in place, that they reflect what truly matters, and that the team is using them to inform decisions. This means encouraging regular conversations about what signals are meaningful, keeping dashboards focused and actionable, and helping the team build habits around learning from data, not just collecting it.

技术负责人在塑造可观测性文化方面扮演着关键角色。你的工作是确保恰当的指标和仪表盘到位、它们反映真正重要的东西、并且团队在用它们来辅助决策。这意味着：鼓励定期讨论哪些信号才有意义，保持仪表盘聚焦且可行动，并帮助团队养成"从数据中学习、而不只是收集数据"的习惯。

— PDF p.306 —

Ensure Quality Through Testing通过测试保障质量

Managing technical projects means driving quality throughout the entire development process. Testing plays a key role, preventing bugs and building confidence in the code, the process, and the team.

管理技术项目，意味着在整个开发过程中推动质量。测试扮演着关键角色：它预防缺陷，并建立起对代码、对流程、对团队的信心。

I already explored in detail how to build and evolve a healthy testing strategy in the section "Continuously Testing" on page 245. If you haven’t read that section yet, that’s where you’ll find actionable guidance on defining testing standards, addressing common bottlenecks like flaky tests and slow pipelines, and building alignment with QA teams.

我已经在第 245 页"持续测试"一节里，详细探讨过如何建立并演进一套健康的测试策略。如果你还没读过那一节，那里有可落地的指引：如何定义测试标准、如何应对不稳定测试和缓慢流水线之类的常见瓶颈，以及如何与 QA 团队建立对齐。

Here, the reminder is this: testing is a continuous investment in quality. Make sure your tests are useful, provide meaningful feedback, are trusted by the team, and support the pace you need to deliver with confidence.

在这里要提醒的是：测试是对质量的一项持续投资。确保你的测试有用、能提供有意义的反馈、被团队信任，并能支撑你有信心交付所需的节奏。

Testing is something you continuously lead. As a tech lead, keep asking yourself: can we release with confidence? If something breaks, will we know? And can we fix it quickly, without blame? The answers to these questions are signals of whether your team has a reliable, quality-focused delivery culture.

测试是你要持续引领的事情。作为技术负责人，不断问自己：我们能有信心地发布吗？如果东西坏了，我们会知道吗？我们能快速修好、而不互相指责吗？这些问题的答案，就是你团队是否拥有可靠的、以质量为核心的交付文化的信号。

If the answer to any of these is no, that signals a broader quality and leadership challenge. You have to make sure testing is a core part of the way work gets done, not something tacked on later. If tests exist but aren’t helpful, or worse, slow things down, question them. If flaky tests are draining trust or key areas of your system lack test coverage, step in. And always make sure your testing approach matches the level of risk in the business and the speed your team is expected to deliver at.

如果其中任何一个答案是否定的，那都意味着一个更大范围的质量与领导力挑战。你必须确保测试是工作方式的核心组成部分，而不是事后才贴上去的东西。如果测试存在却没帮助、甚至拖慢了进度，就要质疑它。如果不稳定的测试正在消耗信任，或系统的关键区域缺乏测试覆盖，就要介入。并且始终确保你的测试方式与业务的风险水平、以及团队被期待的交付速度相匹配。

Testing exists to support delivery. If it’s creating friction instead, that’s a signal to pause, reflect, and adjust it with your team.

测试的存在是为了支撑交付。如果它反而在制造摩擦，那就是一个信号：停下来，反思，和团队一起调整它。

Let the detailed strategies in the section "Continuously Testing" on page 245 guide your implementation. Use this section as a reminder that how well your team tests is a reflection of how well you lead quality.

让第 245 页"持续测试"一节里的详细策略来指导你的落地。把本节当作一句提醒：团队测试做得多好，折射出你引领质量的水平有多高。

Common Project Management Challenges常见项目管理挑战

So far in this chapter, I’ve focused on aligning your team around shared strategies, building a strong technical vision, and encouraging technical excellence through quality, feedback loops, and decision-making practices. But even with all of that in place, projects still go off track. That’s where your role as a tech lead becomes even more critical.

到目前为止，本章聚焦于：让团队围绕共享战略对齐、建立强有力的技术愿景，并通过质量、反馈回路和决策实践来鼓励技术卓越。但即便这一切都到位了，项目仍然会脱轨。这时，你作为技术负责人的角色就变得更加关键。

— PDF p.307 —

In this section, I’ll shift focus to the everyday realities of delivery: how to plan and keep a project on track, how to react when a project starts falling behind, how to juggle multiple streams of work without overwhelming your team, and how to identify and mitigate the technical risks that could quietly derail your delivery.

在本节中，我把焦点转向交付的日常现实：如何规划并让项目不脱轨、当项目开始落后时如何反应、如何在不压垮团队的同时兼顾多条工作流，以及如何识别并缓解那些可能悄悄让你交付脱轨的技术风险。

Strong technical leadership means leading with clarity, navigating complexity, and keeping delivery moving, without burning out your team. You don’t need to become a project manager to do that, but you do need the tools and mindset to guide your team through uncertainty.

强有力的技术领导，意味着以清晰引领、驾驭复杂性、并保持交付向前，同时不把团队耗尽。要做到这一点，你不必变成一名项目经理，但你确实需要相应的工具和心态，来带领团队穿过不确定性。

Planning and Keeping a Project on Track规划并让项目不脱轨

Most projects derail because of bad planning. And bad planning usually comes from a lack of proper communication at the right time between all the parties involved or from a lack of agreement.

大多数项目脱轨，都是因为糟糕的规划。而糟糕的规划，通常源于相关各方在恰当的时机缺乏恰当的沟通，或缺乏共识。

I truly believe the best planning happens when everyone is involved from the beginning: product, business, stakeholders, developers, UX, QA, infrastructure—anyone who touches the product. Maybe not everyone is equally involved at every step, but they should all be present. I’m a big advocate for the whole team being part of this process, not just the tech lead. I’ve seen how much better the outcome is, how much more engaged the team feels, and how much better the product becomes. I’ve seen entire product strategies shift for the better simply because a developer asked a question early on.

我由衷地相信：最好的规划发生在每个人从一开始就参与其中的时候——产品、业务、利益相关者、开发者、UX、QA、基础设施，任何与产品打交道的人。也许不是每个人在每一步都同等深度地参与，但他们都应当在场。我非常主张整个团队都参与这个过程，而不只是技术负责人。我见过结果因此好多少、团队投入度高多少、产品因此好多少。我见过整个产品战略仅仅因为一个开发者早早问了一个问题，就朝更好的方向转变。

But I also know that’s not always the case. In many teams, not even the tech leads are brought into planning. A lot of tech leads still think planning is something product or project managers do and that business will eventually just hand over a list of things to build. That’s how many teams still operate. Unfortunately. And when that happens, it often leads to plans that ignore technical complexity, result in unscalable or overly complex designs, miss important edge cases, or underestimate effort entirely. Without the right voices in the room early, you’re more likely to build the wrong thing, slowly and painfully.

但我也知道，情况并非总是如此。在许多团队里，连技术负责人都没被拉进规划。很多技术负责人仍然以为规划是产品经理或项目经理的事，业务方最终会丢过来一张要做的清单。不幸的是，许多团队至今仍在这样运转。而当这种情况发生时，往往会导致规划忽视技术复杂度、产出不可扩展或过度复杂的设计、漏掉重要的边界情况，或者完全低估工作量。没有恰当的声音早早进入会议室，你更可能缓慢而痛苦地把错误的东西做出来。

If you’re lucky enough to be involved early, great. Take that opportunity. If you’re not, ask why. Often the answer is something like “Oh, I didn’t know you wanted to be involved.” And just like that, you’re in.

如果你够幸运、早早被卷入，很好。抓住这个机会。如果没有，就去问为什么。答案往往是这样的："哦，我不知道你想参与。"就这么简单，你就进来了。

— PDF p.308 —

If you want to maximize the chances of success for any plan your team is leading or involved in, there are a few key things you need to make sure are in place:

如果你想让团队主导或参与的任何计划最大程度地获得成功，有几件关键的事你需要确保到位：

Clear problem to solve / purpose. The best planning starts from a shared understanding of context and purpose:

清晰的待解决问题 / 目的。最好的规划始于对处境和目的的共享理解：

  • Why are we doing this? What’s the problem or opportunity we’re addressing?我们为什么要做这件事？我们要解决的问题或要抓住的机会是什么？
  • Who are the stakeholders? What do they care about? Who will use the solution, approve it, or be affected by it?利益相关者是谁？他们在乎什么？谁会使用这个方案、审批它，或被它影响？
  • What’s the vision? What would success look like, not just in features delivered but in impact created?愿景是什么？成功会是什么样子——不只是交付了哪些功能，还包括创造了什么影响？

From there, the team can envision the shape of the solution, whether that’s architectural direction, key design principles, or a prototype, and only then move toward implementation planning.

在此基础上，团队可以设想方案的形态——无论是架构方向、关键设计原则，还是一个原型——然后才进入实现层面的规划。

Clear owner. I once helped a startup troubleshoot why a company-level project had missed its deadline by three months. The project involved three different engineering teams. My first question was simple: who owned this project? The responses revealed the core issue. The tech lead assumed the product manager was in charge. The product manager thought it was the engineering manager’s responsibility. The EM pointed to the CTO. And the team believed the tech lead was managing it. Everyone assumed someone else was driving, but no one ever said it out loud.

清晰的负责人。我曾帮一家初创公司排查：为什么一个公司级项目晚了三个月才交付。这个项目涉及三个不同的工程团队。我的第一个问题很简单：这个项目归谁负责？大家的回答暴露了核心问题。技术负责人以为产品经理在管，产品经理以为这是工程经理的责任，工程经理把手指向 CTO，而团队则以为是技术负责人在管。每个人都以为别人在推动，但谁也没把它说出口。

The result? No one had a full picture of what was happening. There was no shared timeline, no one enforcing the deadline, and each team was planning and prioritizing independently on different boards. Nobody was coordinating the bigger picture.

结果呢？没有人掌握全貌。没有共享的时间线，没有人在督促截止日期，每个团队都在不同的看板上独立地规划、排优先级。没有人在协调大局。

The lesson was clear: when everyone is responsible, no one is.

教训很清楚：当人人都负责时，就没人负责了。

— PDF p.309 —

One of the most common reasons I’ve seen tech projects and initiatives fail is the absence of clear ownership. You need one single point of contact: someone responsible for tracking progress, updating communications, following up on decisions, and reacting when things go off track.

我见过技术项目和举措失败，最常见的原因之一就是缺乏清晰的归属。你需要一个单一的对接人：有人负责追踪进展、更新沟通、跟进决策，并在事情脱轨时做出反应。

Owners aren’t expected to do everything themselves or be present in every meeting. Their role is to provide visibility into the plan, tracking progress, highlighting risks, and making sure responsibilities are clearly understood. With the right structure in place, the team should be able to move forward independently, without needing constant supervision.

负责人不必什么都自己做，也不必每场会都在场。他们的角色是：让计划可见、追踪进展、突出风险，并确保职责被清晰理解。有了恰当的结构，团队应当能够独立前进，而不需要持续的监督。

Clear steps. Break down the work into tangible, achievable chunks. Each step should be actionable and easy to understand. Avoid vague labels like “implement feature.” Instead, be specific: “build endpoint for X” or “create UI component for Y.” This helps the team track progress and makes handoffs smoother.

清晰的步骤。把工作拆成有形的、可达成的小块。每个步骤都应当可执行、易理解。避免"实现功能"这种含糊的标签。相反，要具体："为 X 构建接口"或"为 Y 创建 UI 组件"。这帮助团队追踪进展，也让交接更顺畅。

At the high level, start with stakeholder conversations and product goals, then shape these into large epics that reflect business priorities. From there, work with your team to split those epics into smaller tasks that can be executed within your sprint cycles.

在高层，从与利益相关者的对话和产品目标出发，把它们塑造成反映业务优先级的大型史诗（epic）。然后和团队一起，把这些史诗拆成可以在 sprint 周期内执行的小任务。

Keeping this dual-layer structure, strategic (epic-level) and tactical (task-level), helps ensure everyone from business to engineering stays aligned on both the big picture and the next step.

保持这种双层结构——战略层（史诗级）和战术层（任务级——有助于确保从业务到工程的每个人，在大局和下一步上都保持对齐。

Clear milestones. Define what success looks like at various points in the project. These are your checkpoints, moments where you pause, reflect, and potentially readjust. Milestones might signal the end of a sprint, the completion of a critical feature, or the delivery of a first internal demo. They help track progress, but more importantly, they create space to check alignment, surface risks, and make informed adjustments. Choose milestones that show meaningful progress, especially to stakeholders, and use them to validate or update your delivery plans.

清晰的里程碑。定义在项目的各个节点上成功是什么样子。这些就是你的检查点——你停下来、反思、并可能重新调整的时刻。里程碑可以标志一个 sprint 的结束、一个关键功能的完成，或第一次内部演示的交付。它们帮助追踪进展，但更重要的是，它们创造了空间去检查对齐、暴露风险、并做出有依据的调整。选择那些能展现有意义进展的里程碑——尤其是对利益相关者而言——并用它们来验证或更新你的交付计划。

Clear timelines. I’ve seen tech leads hesitate to enforce timelines, worried they’ll come across as pushy or create pressure on the team. So instead, they say nothing. They go with the flow, hoping things will somehow be delivered on time.

清晰的时间线。我见过技术负责人不敢去督促时间线，担心自己显得强势、或给团队制造压力。于是他们什么也不说。随波逐流，盼着事情不知怎么就能按时交付。

— PDF p.310 —

But the truth is there is always a timeline. The business side always has expectations about when they want something delivered. If it’s not clearly stated, ask for it, and don’t give up until you get a real answer.

但真相是：时间线永远存在。业务方对"什么时候想要某个东西交付"总有预期。如果它没被明说出来，就去问，而且不得到一个真实的答案绝不罢休。

If you struggle to get one, propose your own. Start by giving an intentionally long estimate, something you know won’t be acceptable, like “OK, so we’ll aim to get this done in about six months.” Chances are, you’ll get a reaction: “Six months?! That’s way too long.” Perfect. Now you can ask: “What would be acceptable?” Maybe they say, “We were hoping for three.” Great. Now you have a target and something to plan around.

如果你实在问不出来，就自己提一个。先故意给一个很长的、你知道不会被接受的估计，比如："那我们争取大约六个月把它做完吧。"很可能你会得到这样的反应："六个月？！那也太久了。"太好了。现在你可以问："那多久可以接受？"也许他们会说："我们本来希望三个月。"很好。现在你有了一个目标，有了可以围绕它做规划的东西。

If it’s not clearly stated, it becomes invisible. And when it’s invisible, people assume they have all the time in the world. That’s when you end up with someone refactoring a huge piece of the product in what was meant to be a small task. Without clear boundaries, people set their own. And everyone’s idea of a reasonable timeline is different.

如果它没被明说出来，它就变得不可见。而当它不可见时，人们就以为自己有的是时间。这时你就会看到：有人在一个本应很小的任务里，去重构产品的一大块。没有清晰的边界，人们就会自己划边界。而每个人对"合理时间线"的理解都不一样。

I remember working with a tech lead who was anxious about an upcoming delivery. Her team was behind schedule. Stakeholders were checking in constantly. She felt the pressure mounting but didn’t want to push the team. “What’s the actual deadline?” I asked. “There isn’t one,” she said. “But everyone expects it by May 1st.”

我记得和一位技术负责人共事，她为即将到来的交付焦虑不已。她的团队进度落后。利益相关者不断来问。她感到压力越来越大，但又不想逼团队。"真正的截止日期是什么时候？"我问。"没有截止日期，"她说，"但大家都期望 5 月 1 号之前。"

“So there is a deadline,” I said. “It just hasn’t been made explicit.” I suggested she share that with her team, not as a demand but as transparency. Just share that there’s an expectation, explain why it matters, and bring the team into the strategy conversation.

"那就是有截止日期，"我说，"只是没被明说出来。"我建议她把这件事和团队分享——不是作为命令，而是作为透明。就只是告诉大家有这么一个预期、解释它为什么重要，并把团队带进战略讨论里。

She did. In our next one-on-one, she said, “That worked like magic. Once I explained the situation, the team prioritized the work together. We’re actually ahead of schedule now.”

她照做了。在我们下一次一对一沟通时，她说："这招像施了魔法一样。我一解释情况，团队就一起排了优先级。我们现在其实还提前了。"

This is the power of clear expectations. When people understand the “why,” they align fast.

这就是清晰预期的力量。当人们理解了"为什么"，他们对齐得很快。

The key is to treat deadlines and milestones as shared goals, not demands. “We want to finish this by May 1st because of X.” Then open the conversation. Is that realistic? Can we shift it? What’s the impact if we don’t? On us, on the customer, on the business? If the timeline is fixed, can we adjust the scope? What’s the smallest version we could ship that still brings value? Could part of it be manual for now?

关键是把截止日期和里程碑当作共享的目标，而不是命令。"因为 X，我们想在 5 月 1 号之前完成。"然后打开对话。那现实吗？能挪吗？如果做不到会有什么影响？对我们、对客户、对业务？如果时间线是固定的，我们能调整范围吗？我们能交付的、仍能带来价值的最小版本是什么？其中一部分暂时用手工方式处理行不行？

Creating this plan doesn’t fall entirely on your shoulders, and usually you are not the one that drives it. In most teams, it’s a shared effort between you and your product owner, product manager, project manager, engineering manager, or whoever else is involved. You all bring something different to the table. Your role is to contribute the technical perspective: how feasible things are, where the risks lie, how the team works in practice. Their role is to bring business context, customer needs, and priorities. Together, you’re jointly responsible for making sure the team has a clear, realistic path forward.

制定这份计划并不全压在你肩上，通常你也不是那个推动它的人。在大多数团队里，这是你和产品负责人、产品经理、项目经理、工程经理，或任何其他相关者共同的努力。你们各自带来不同的东西。你的角色是贡献技术视角：事情有多可行、风险在哪里、团队实际是怎么工作的。他们的角色是带来业务语境、客户需求和优先级。你们共同负责，确保团队有一条清晰、现实的前进道路。

— PDF p.311 —

A clear plan also enables speed. Once your team moves into execution, they should know exactly what they’re working on and why. Nothing hurts productivity more than lack of focus.

一份清晰的计划还能带来速度。一旦团队进入执行，他们应当确切地知道自己在做什么、以及为什么做。没有什么比缺乏专注更伤害生产力了。

I once joined a team full of motivated, capable engineers who were struggling to deliver, not because they lacked skills but because they lacked clarity. The backlog was messy, stories were vague, and tasks were made up as they went. Junior developers were blocked, waiting for direction.

我曾加入过一个团队，里面全是积极、能干的工程师，却挣扎着交付不出来——不是因为缺技能，而是因为缺清晰。待办列表一团乱，用户故事含糊不清，任务是走一步编一步。初级开发者被卡住，等着人给方向。

When I joined as a tech lead, I quickly realized this wasn’t a problem of motivation or talent; it was a planning problem. There was a product manager, but she was stretched thin, managing multiple teams and projects, and didn’t have the capacity to go deep into the day-to-day planning. So instead of jumping straight into the code, I dove into the backlog. I started working closely with the product manager, legal department, and other teams involved, helping shape a clear high-level strategy. I set up planning ceremonies like pre-planning and refinement sessions and brought the team into the process.

当我以技术负责人身份加入时，很快意识到这不是动力或天赋的问题，而是规划问题。团队里有一位产品经理，但她分身乏术，管着好几个团队和项目，没有精力深入到日常规划里。于是我没有直接扑进代码，而是扎进了待办列表。我开始和产品经理、法务部门以及其他相关团队紧密合作，帮助塑造一套清晰的高层战略。我设立了规划仪式，比如预规划和需求细化会，并把团队带进这个过程。

In just a month, everything changed. The team was thriving. Work was moving fast, confidently. No second-guessing, no confusion, just clear priorities, a shared process, and a rhythm for getting things done. Once all of that was in place, once we had a clear plan, a clear timeline, and full alignment, I finally went hands-on to help deliver. Because at that point, the team had the structure and clarity they needed to actually move fast. Planning is what made that possible.

仅仅一个月，一切都变了。团队生机勃勃。工作快速而自信地推进。不再自我怀疑，不再困惑，只有清晰的优先级、共享的流程，以及把事情做完的节奏。当这一切都到位——当我们有了清晰的计划、清晰的时间线、完全的对齐——我才终于亲手下场帮忙交付。因为到那时，团队已经拥有了真正快速前进所需的结构和清晰。是规划让这一切成为可能。

Another thing that kills focus is trying to do too much at once. If everything is a priority, nothing gets done. A common trap for teams is having too many work items in progress at the same time, resulting in jumping between tasks, starting but not finishing, and losing track of priorities. That’s why part of effective planning is limiting WIP (work in progress).

另一个扼杀专注的，是试图同时做太多事。如果样样都是优先，就样样都做不成。团队常见的一个陷阱是：同时进行太多工作项，结果在任务之间跳来跳去、开了头却收不了尾，还忘了优先级。这就是为什么有效规划的一部分，是限制 WIP（在制品，work in progress）。

Help your team stay focused by agreeing on how much work can be in motion at once. Encourage finishing over starting. Before picking up a new task from the to-do list, pause and talk about trade-offs, especially if there are still plenty of tasks in progress. In one of my teams, we had this principle so deeply embedded that if the board was full of in-progress tasks, no one would start something new. Instead, anyone without a task would pair with someone else to help finish what was already underway.

帮助团队保持专注，办法是就"同时能推进多少工作"达成一致。鼓励"完成"胜过"开始"。在从待办列表里接新任务之前，先停下来谈谈权衡——尤其是当还有一大堆任务在进行中时。在我带过的一个团队里，这条原则深入人心：如果看板上全是进行中的任务，就没人会开新的头。相反，手头没任务的人会去和别人结对，帮忙把已经在做的事情收尾。

To wrap up, treat planning as a tool for collaboration. Great planning builds shared understanding, aligns expectations, and creates space for ongoing recalibration. That means having regular conversations at both strategic and tactical levels, with stakeholders, your team, and anyone whose work intersects with yours. When you lead planning this way, you’ll catch risks earlier, adjust faster, and build better things together.

总结一句：把规划当作协作的工具。好的规划建立共享理解、对齐预期，并为持续的重新校准创造空间。这意味着在战略和战术两个层面，与利益相关者、你的团队、以及任何与你工作有交集的人，保持定期对话。当你这样引领规划时，你会更早发现风险、更快调整，并一起把东西做得更好。

— PDF p.312 —

Plans should be visible, dynamic, and shared.

计划应当是看得见的、动态的、被共享的。

Responding to Project Delays应对项目延期

Even with the best planning, things will go wrong. An incident might hit. Someone gets sick. You run into a technical complexity you underestimated. Or a third-party dependency slips.

即便做了最好的规划，事情也会出岔子。可能撞上一次事故。可能有人病倒。可能遇到了你低估的技术复杂度。也可能某个第三方依赖掉了链子。

That’s normal. What matters is how you respond.

这都很正常。重要的是你如何回应。

First thing to do as a tech lead: make the risk visible. The moment you suspect a delay or see something slipping, your first responsibility is to make the risk apparent. Don’t wait. Share it with your team, your stakeholders, and anyone else who might be affected. Then bring everyone together to revisit the plan. Can you shift the timeline? Trim scope? Deliver part of the work manually for now?

作为技术负责人，第一件事：让风险变得可见。一旦你察觉到延期、或看到事情在滑落，你的首要责任就是把这个风险摆上台面。别等。把它告诉团队、告诉利益相关者、告诉任何可能受影响的人。然后把大家聚在一起重新审视计划。你能挪动时间线吗？能砍范围吗？能不能暂时先用手工方式交付一部分？

In one project, we were launching a new product that had already been sold to customers with a promised start date. Two weeks before launch, we realized the third-party API we were relying on wouldn’t be ready in time. Postponing wasn’t an option, so we got creative with scope.

有一个项目，我们正要上线一个新产品，它已经卖给了客户、并承诺了一个开始日期。上线前两周，我们意识到所依赖的第三方 API 没法按时就绪。延期不是选项，于是我们在范围上动起了脑筋。

We identified the minimum set of features that absolutely needed to work automatically. Then, we renegotiated with the third-party provider to deliver a smaller, stripped-down version of the API that could support just those essentials.

我们找出了那组"必须自动运行"的最小功能集。然后和第三方供应商重新谈判，让他们交付一个更小、精简版的 API，只支持那些最基本的功能。

For one feature, we made a conscious decision to handle it manually at first. It wasn’t scalable long term, but with only a handful of early clients and the feature being triggered manually, it was totally manageable. We added a flag to indicate when the manual process was needed, and aligned with the PM on a follow-up plan to automate it down the line.

对其中一个功能，我们有意识地决定先手工处理。它长期看不可扩展，但因为早期客户只有寥寥几个、且这个功能是手工触发的，完全管得过来。我们加了一个标记，用来指示何时需要走手工流程，并和产品经理就"日后把它自动化"的后续计划达成了一致。

The launch went smoothly thanks to our ability to adapt quickly, communicate clearly, and make thoughtful trade-offs, even under pressure.

上线很顺利，这要归功于我们快速适应、清晰沟通、以及即便在压力下也能做出深思熟虑的权衡的能力。

You’re not responsible for solving every problem alone. Your focus is on maintaining alignment across people and priorities: keeping communication open, translating business goals into delivery plans, and ensuring the team understands what’s expected before it becomes a surprise.

你没有责任独自解决每一个问题。你的焦点是在人和优先级之间维持对齐：保持沟通畅通、把业务目标翻译成交付计划，并确保团队在"变成一个意外"之前就明白期待是什么。

Also, be careful with the idea of “just adding more people.” When a deadline is at risk, stakeholders often say, “Can’t we just add more developers?” On the surface, it sounds like a quick fix. It sounds logical: more hands, faster delivery. But in reality, onboarding new developers slows things down.
