Not only do they need to learn the codebase; they need to learn how your team works, how you collaborate, how you deploy.

另外，要小心"再加点人不就行了"这种想法。当截止日期有风险时，利益相关者常说："我们不能多加点开发者吗？"表面上，这听起来像个快速修复。逻辑上也说得通：人手越多，交付越快。但实际上，让新开发者上手会拖慢进度。他们不仅要学代码库，还要学你们团队怎么工作、怎么协作、怎么部署。

— PDF p.313 —

It’s like the old saying: what one developer can do in one day, two can do in two days. Unless you’re already set up to scale with new people, it’s rarely a quick fix.

就像那句老话：一个开发者一天能做完的事，两个人要两天。除非你本来就搭建好了"随新人扩展"的条件，否则它很少是个快速修复。

Second thing to do as a tech lead: protect the team’s focus. As a tech lead, part of your job is to shield the team from distractions and last-minute “urgent” requests that pop up mid-sprint. You won’t be able to block every interruption, but you can create clarity around what the team is working on and why.

作为技术负责人，第二件事：保护团队的专注。作为技术负责人，你的部分工作是为团队挡掉干扰，以及 sprint 中途冒出来的"紧急"临时请求。你挡不住每一次打扰，但你可以让团队正在做什么、为什么做，变得清晰。

Without this kind of buffer, teams can fall into what some call the “interrupt-driven death spiral,” constantly reacting and context switching and never finishing meaningful work. Make sure that doesn’t happen.

没有这种缓冲，团队就可能掉进有人所说的"中断驱动的死亡螺旋"：不停地反应、不停地切换上下文，却永远完不成有意义的工作。一定要确保别让这种事发生。

Make your priorities visible. Encourage your team to talk openly about priorities when unexpected tasks get thrown their way, and to explore options like saying “Not right now, because we’re focused on delivering X” or “Let’s put it in the backlog and we’ll revisit later,” rather than jumping in automatically.

让你的优先级看得见。鼓励团队在被塞来意外任务时，公开地谈论优先级，并去探索这样的选项："现在不行，因为我们正专注于交付 X"，或"先放进待办列表，以后再看"——而不是自动地跳进去。

If you don’t set these boundaries, everything becomes a priority, and then nothing gets done on time. Being the buffer between the team and the chaos is one of the most valuable ways you support delivery.

如果你不设这些边界，就会样样都成了优先，结果样样都不能按时完成。做团队与混乱之间的缓冲，是你支撑交付最有价值的方式之一。

Another thing to keep in mind during these pressure situations: checking in on morale. When a project’s behind, stress rises. Tensions run high. In moments like this, one-on-ones are your best friend. Use them to check how people are feeling. Are they worried? Burned out? Feeling stuck or unsupported? This is where you catch problems before they explode. These conversations help you know when to push, when to shield, and when to pause and reassess.

在这种高压局面下还要记住一件事：关注士气。当项目落后时，压力上升，情绪紧绷。这种时候，一对一沟通是你最好的朋友。用它来了解大家的感受。他们在担心吗？耗竭了吗？觉得卡住了、或不被支持吗？正是在这里，你能在问题爆炸之前抓住它。这些对话帮你知道：什么时候该推一把、什么时候该挡一下、什么时候该停下来重新评估。

In short, when a project slips, don’t panic. Slow down. Communicate. Recalibrate. And support your team. That’s how you keep moving forward without losing trust or burning out your people.

简而言之，当项目滑落时，别慌。慢下来。去沟通。重新校准。并支持你的团队。这样你才能在不失去信任、不把人耗尽的前提下，继续前进。

Balancing Multiple Streams of Work平衡多条工作流

If your team owns a single product with clear boundaries, the same tech stack, familiar tooling, and consistent services, you’re in a fortunate position. Many tech teams today aren’t that lucky. It’s increasingly common for tech teams to be responsible for multiple products or projects spread across different systems, services, programming languages, and infrastructure. And this comes with a cost.

如果你的团队只负责一个产品，边界清晰、技术栈相同、工具熟悉、服务稳定，那你处境很幸运。如今许多技术团队没这个运气。技术团队要负责分布在不同系统、服务、编程语言和基础设施上的多个产品或项目，这种情况越来越常见。而这是有代价的。

Everything takes longer than planned: onboarding, maintenance, debugging. The biggest challenge is context switching. Jumping between tech stacks or products drains focus and energy. It slows the team down and makes execution more difficult.

一切都比计划更耗时：上手、维护、调试。最大的挑战是上下文切换。在技术栈或产品之间跳来跳去，会消耗专注力和精力。它拖慢团队，让执行变得更难。

— PDF p.314 —

I’ve been there. My team was responsible for two completely different products, both high-priority, both business-critical. But one lived in a legacy .NET monolith running in a datacenter with RabbitMQ and MySQL. The other was a modern Scala-based microservice using Kafka streams and DynamoDB and deployed in AWS. The mental overhead of switching between these two worlds was enormous.

我经历过。我的团队负责两个完全不同的产品，都是高优先级、都是业务关键。但一个住在数据中心里的老旧 .NET 单体中，用的是 RabbitMQ 和 MySQL；另一个是现代的、基于 Scala 的微服务，用 Kafka streams 和 DynamoDB，部署在 AWS。在这两个世界之间切换的精神负担是巨大的。

And yet, we made it work, by factoring this challenge into how we worked as a team.

尽管如此，我们还是让它运转起来了——办法是把这个挑战纳入我们团队的工作方式里去考量。

We used tools to reduce context-switching friction: things like clear onboarding guides, well-maintained internal wikis, and architecture diagrams that gave fast overviews of the systems involved. This was not a setup where relying on code for documentation alone was an option.

我们用工具来降低上下文切换的摩擦：比如清晰的上手指南、维护良好的内部 wiki，以及能快速概览相关系统的架构图。在这种局面下，"只靠代码来当文档"根本行不通。

Our delivery process was smooth, built on continuous deployment and supported by thorough testing and strict quality standards. We explicitly accounted for context switching in our estimates, acknowledging that jumping between products carried a cost.

我们的交付流程很顺畅，建立在持续部署之上，并由充分的测试和严格的质量标准支撑。我们在估算中显式地把上下文切换算进去，承认在产品之间切换是有代价的。

We also leaned heavily on pair programming. Any time someone had to switch to the other product, they weren’t doing it alone; there was always someone else to carry the context, ease the transition, and help get up to speed. Constant, structured communication helped keep us aligned, internally and with stakeholders. We maintained a clear sense of strategy and focus.

我们还大量依赖结对编程。每当有人要切到另一个产品时，他不是单打独斗；总有另一个人帮他带着上下文、缓冲切换、并帮他快速上手。持续而结构化的沟通，帮助我们在内部、以及与利益相关者之间保持对齐。我们保持了清晰的战略感和专注。

I also was regularly checking in with the team to make sure this approach was still working. Was the context switching becoming too much? Were people feeling overwhelmed? These conversations helped us stay ahead of problems before they grew. I knew that what worked at one point might stop working as priorities shifted.

我还定期和团队沟通，确认这套做法是否仍然有效。上下文切换是不是太多了？大家是不是觉得吃不消？这些对话帮助我们在问题长大之前就抢先一步。我知道：在某个时点有效的做法，随着优先级变化可能会失效。

Even with all this, it was hard. We struggled from time to time. But we approached it as a learning opportunity. Where else could we have explored two completely different technology stacks, back-to-back, as part of the same team? It stretched us, but it also grew us.

即便做了这一切，它仍然很难。我们时不时地挣扎。但我们把它当作一次学习机会。还有哪里能让我们作为同一个团队，背靠背地探索两套完全不同的技术栈呢？它拉伸了我们，但也让我们成长。

— PDF p.315 —

There are a few other approaches I’ve seen work well for other teams in similar situations.

我还见过其他一些做法，在处境类似的团队中效果不错。

Clarify ownership boundaries up front. One of the most helpful things you can do is explicitly define who owns what. Which team is responsible for which product or service? What does that ownership include—feature work, support, maintenance? Where do responsibilities stop? This removes ambiguity and helps avoid surprises when work overlaps.

事先厘清归属边界。你能做的最有用的事情之一，就是明确定义谁负责什么。哪个团队负责哪个产品或服务？这种归属包括什么——功能开发、支持、维护？责任到哪里为止？这消除了模糊性，并在工作重叠时避免意外。

Instead of juggling both products at the same time, you can place one product into full maintenance mode temporarily, agreeing to handle only critical bugs or issues, while prioritizing the other for a defined period. This would allow deeper focus without letting anything fall through the cracks.

与其同时兼顾两个产品，你可以暂时把一个产品置于完全维护模式——约定只处理关键缺陷或问题，同时在一段既定时间内优先做另一个。这样能让你更深入地专注，又不会让任何东西从缝隙里掉下去。

Proactively challenge the assumption that your team has to keep owning everything. If the load is too high, it’s OK to hand something off. A clear, structured handover to another team, or even a temporary reallocation of ownership, can create space to breathe. In our case, we had this conversation and decided we wanted to keep both.

主动去挑战"你的团队必须一直负责一切"这个假设。如果负荷太高，把东西交出去是完全可以的。一次清晰、结构化的向另一个团队的交接，甚至一次临时的归属再分配，都能创造出喘息的空间。在我们的例子里，我们做了这场对话，并决定两个都要保留。

I’ve also heard of teams using rotating sub-teams or specializations to manage multiple projects, though I haven’t tried it myself. The idea is to split the team temporarily—one group focuses on Product A, another on Product B—then rotate members regularly. It’s supposed to reduce context switching while spreading knowledge gradually. Seems like a smart way to balance focus and flexibility.

我还听说有些团队用"轮换子团队"或"专业化分工"来管理多个项目，不过我自己没试过。思路是把团队临时拆分——一组专注产品 A，另一组专注产品 B——然后定期轮换成员。它的目的是在逐步扩散知识的同时减少上下文切换。看起来像是平衡专注与灵活的聪明做法。

And of course, escalate early. If your team is overwhelmed, don’t keep it to yourself. Talk to your stakeholders. Show them the impact of divided attention: slower delivery, more bugs, rising frustration. Bring the problem to light while there’s still time to do something about it.

当然，还有：尽早升级。如果你的团队吃不消了，别自己憋着。去和利益相关者谈。给他们看看分散注意力的影响：更慢的交付、更多的缺陷、不断上升的挫败感。趁还有时间做点什么的时候，把问题摆上台面。

Balancing multiple streams of work will never be easy. But with clear priorities, deliberate trade-offs, and a willingness to set boundaries, it becomes manageable. If you’re in this situation now, take a moment to assess, then try one of these adjustments. It might be just what your team needs.

平衡多条工作流永远不会容易。但有了清晰的优先级、有意识的权衡、以及设定边界的意愿，它就变得可管理。如果你现在正处在这种处境里，花一点时间评估一下，然后试试其中一个调整。那也许正是你的团队所需要的。

— PDF p.316 —

Managing Technical Risk管理技术风险

Every project comes with risks. Your role as a tech lead is to ensure these risks don’t transform into issues.

每个项目都伴随着风险。作为技术负责人，你的角色是确保这些风险不会演变成问题。

A risk is something that might happen. It’s a potential issue. For example: “A server crash during peak hours might lead to data loss.”

风险，是可能发生的事情。它是一个潜在的问题。例如："高峰时段服务器崩溃，可能导致数据丢失。"

An issue, on the other hand, is something that has already happened, like a problem in production. For example: “During peak hours, the search page takes four times longer to load.”

而问题（issue），是已经发生了的事情，比如生产环境里的一个故障。例如："高峰时段，搜索页面加载时间变成了平时的四倍。"

Issues are dealt with reactively: you fix them, work around them, or accept them. For instance, you might increase the number of search servers temporarily to reduce load time. For a longer-term solution, you could restructure the search index to better match common user queries. In some cases, the best choice might be to simply acknowledge the issue, such as showing users a message when search is slow, especially if the impact is minor and the cost to fix is too high right now.

问题是被动应对的：你修复它、绕开它，或接受它。比如，你可以临时增加搜索服务器的数量来降低加载时间。作为更长期的方案，你可以重构搜索索引，让它更好地匹配常见的用户查询。在某些情况下，最好的选择也许就是承认这个问题——比如在搜索慢时给用户一条提示——尤其是当影响很小、而眼下修复成本又太高的时候。

Risks, however, must be identified, tracked, communicated, and planned for.

而风险，则必须被识别、追踪、沟通，并为之做好计划。

Identifying risks识别风险

Every project comes with risks, and no, you won’t be able to mitigate them all. But you can make them visible and prepare for the most critical ones using different techniques.

每个项目都有风险，而且，你没法把它们全部缓解掉。但你可以让它们变得可见，并用不同的技术为最关键的那些做好准备。

One useful technique is Agile threat modeling, which focuses on identifying security risks. Some companies have a dedicated security team, but they’re often stretched thin. That means security reviews come too late, miss key context, or rely on noisy automated tools.

一个有用的技术是敏捷威胁建模（Agile threat modeling），它聚焦于识别安全风险。有些公司有专门的安全团队，但他们常常分身乏术。这意味着安全评审来得太晚、漏掉关键语境，或依赖吵吵闹闹的自动化工具。

Agile threat modeling flips that: it’s done more frequently, in smaller chunks, and involves the whole team. It becomes part of your backlog and planning. I first encountered this practice at Thoughtworks. They’ve even published a full guide on how to run one: the Agile Threat Modelling Workshop Guide.

敏捷威胁建模把它翻转过来：它更频繁地进行、拆成小块、并让整个团队参与。它成为你待办列表和规划的一部分。我第一次是在 Thoughtworks 接触到这种做法。他们甚至还出版了一本完整的指南，讲如何开展：《Agile Threat Modelling Workshop Guide》。

Another excellent tool is risk-storming. It’s a collaborative, visual exercise where the whole team, devs, project managers, product managers, designers, and stakeholders identify risks together. You map them out, prioritize them, and discuss mitigation strategies. The guide at riskstorming.com is a great place to start.

另一个极好的工具是风险风暴（risk-storming）。它是一种协作式、可视化的练习：整个团队——开发者、项目经理、产品经理、设计师和利益相关者——一起识别风险。你把它们画出来、排优先级、并讨论缓解策略。riskstorming.com 上的指南是很好的起点。

And if you’ve been maintaining a RAID board (risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies) throughout your decision-making or solution brainstorming sessions, this is a great moment to bring it up again. It can provide a clear view of previously identified risks and ensure continuity in addressing them proactively.

而如果你在做决策或方案头脑风暴时，一直维护着一块 RAID 看板（风险、假设、问题、依赖），那现在正是把它重新拿出来的好时机。它能让你清晰看到此前识别出的风险，并确保在主动应对它们时保持连续性。

Identifying risks should be a regular part of your project rhythm. A good rule of thumb is to consider risks at the following times:

识别风险应当成为你项目节奏中的常规一环。一个好的经验法则是，在以下时点考虑风险：

  • At the start of a project, to uncover early architectural or security concerns在项目开始时，及早暴露架构或安全方面的顾虑
  • Before major milestones or deliveries, to prepare for potential blockers在重要里程碑或交付之前，为潜在的阻塞做好准备
  • After significant changes in direction or scope, when new risks often appear在方向或范围发生重大变化之后——这时往往会冒出新的风险
  • On a regular cadence, such as monthly or at the start of each sprint cycle, to keep the conversation alive按固定节奏，比如每月、或每个 sprint 周期开始时，让这场讨论持续进行
— PDF p.317 —

You don’t need to run a full workshop every time. Sometimes a quick review of your existing risks and assumptions is enough.

你不必每次都办一场完整的工作坊。有时，快速回顾一下你现有的风险和假设就够了。

Mitigating risks缓解风险

Once you’ve identified your risks, you need to evaluate them. A common way to do this is using a 2 × 2 matrix:

一旦识别出风险，你就需要评估它们。一个常见的做法是用一个 2×2 矩阵：

  • Probability: How likely is this to happen?可能性：它发生的概率有多大？
  • Impact: If it does happen, how bad is it?影响：如果它真的发生，会有多糟？

Based on those two factors, you can choose a mitigation strategy (Figure 9-1).

根据这两个因素，你就可以选择一种缓解策略（见图 9-1）。

You can choose to mitigate, avoid, accept, or transfer the risk:

你可以选择缓解、规避、接受，或转移这个风险：

Mitigate. Take steps to reduce the likelihood or impact.

缓解（Mitigate）。采取措施降低它发生的可能性或影响。

Example: You rely on a third-party payment provider, and downtime on their end would block customers from completing purchases. You mitigate this risk by building a lightweight fallback system: when the provider is down, customers can still place orders, and payments are processed once the service is restored.

示例：你依赖一家第三方支付服务商，而他们那边一旦宕机，就会挡住客户完成购买。你通过搭建一个轻量的兜底系统来缓解这个风险：当服务商宕机时，客户仍然可以下单，等服务恢复后再处理支付。

You can’t eliminate the risk of the third-party service failing, but you reduce its impact on the business. Instead of losing revenue or frustrating users during downtime, you create a way to keep things moving while minimizing disruption.

你无法消除第三方服务故障的风险，但你降低了它对业务的影响。与其在宕机期间损失收入、或让用户沮丧，不如创造一种方式，在把扰动降到最小的同时让事情继续转下去。

— PDF p.318 —

Avoid. Change your approach so the risk no longer applies.

规避（Avoid）。改变你的做法，让这个风险不再适用。

Example: You were planning to allow users to upload and preview arbitrary file types in your application. But this opens up a range of risks, like malicious file uploads, virus-laden attachments, or vulnerabilities in previewing logic.

示例：你原本计划允许用户在应用里上传并预览任意类型的文件。但这会打开一系列风险，比如恶意文件上传、带病毒的附件，或预览逻辑里的漏洞。

After assessing the effort required to scan and sanitize all file types securely, you change the approach: users can upload only PDFs, which are stored without preview and scanned with a standard antivirus tool before storage.

在评估了"安全地扫描并清洗所有文件类型"所需的工作量之后，你改变了做法：用户只能上传 PDF，PDF 不做预览，并在存储前用标准杀毒工具扫描。

Allowing arbitrary file uploads introduces complex security concerns that are difficult to fully mitigate. By narrowing the scope to a safer file type and removing the preview feature, you avoid exposing your system to these risks altogether.

允许任意文件上传会引入复杂的安全顾虑，很难被彻底缓解。通过把范围收窄到一种更安全的文件类型、并去掉预览功能，你就让系统完全暴露于这些风险之外。

Accept. You’re aware of the risk but decide not to act, at least for now.

接受（Accept）。你意识到这个风险，但决定不采取行动——至少眼下如此。

Example: You know your CI pipeline is slower than ideal, but improving it would require infrastructure changes that aren’t a priority right now.

示例：你知道你的 CI 流水线比理想的慢，但改进它需要改动基础设施，而这眼下不是优先事项。

You’re aware this might lead to longer feedback loops for developers and reduced iteration speed. It could eventually affect team morale or delivery timelines. But for now, the impact is manageable, so you choose to accept the risk, monitor it, and set a reminder to visit it in some time.

你意识到这可能导致开发者的反馈回路更长、迭代速度下降。它最终可能影响团队士气或交付时间线。但眼下影响是可控的，所以你选择接受这个风险、监控它，并设一个提醒，过段时间再来处理。

Transfer. Shift responsibility elsewhere, like outsourcing or involving another team.

转移（Transfer）。把责任转移到别处，比如外包，或让另一个团队接手。

Example: You’re worried about the security risks in handling user authentication in-house. Instead of building and maintaining your own auth system, you decide to use a third-party identity provider.

示例：你担心自己在内部处理用户认证的安全风险。于是你决定使用第三方身份服务商，而不是自己构建和维护一套认证系统。

You’re aware that authentication is a critical and sensitive area; getting it wrong could lead to security breaches and compliance issues. But instead of carrying that risk internally, you transfer it to a provider with better expertise, support, and security practices in this area.

你知道认证是一个关键而敏感的领域；一旦出错，可能导致安全漏洞和合规问题。但你没有把这个风险扛在内部，而是把它转移给了一家在这个领域拥有更好专业能力、支持和安全实践的服务商。

Choosing how to respond to risk is just as important as identifying it. Whether you accept, transfer, mitigate, or avoid a risk, the key is to do it intentionally, with a clear understanding of the trade-offs involved.

选择如何回应风险，和识别风险同样重要。无论你是接受、转移、缓解还是规避一个风险，关键是要带着对其中权衡的清晰理解，有意识地去做。

Not every risk needs action right away, but every risk needs visibility and ownership.

不是每个风险都需要立刻行动，但每个风险都需要被看见、并有人负责。

— PDF p.319 —

Tracking risks追踪风险

After a risk-storming or threat modeling session, you’ll have a list of prioritized risks. But that’s just the beginning. You need to track them.

在一次风险风暴或威胁建模会议之后，你会得到一份排好优先级的风险清单。但这只是开始。你需要追踪它们。

A risk log can be a Google Doc, a Jira board, or a spreadsheet; it doesn’t matter, as long as it’s reviewed regularly. Each risk is clearly described and easy to refer to in conversation. The mitigation plan and current status are kept visible so that anyone on the team can quickly understand where things stand. And each risk has a clear owner—not necessarily the person executing the work but someone responsible for making sure it’s tracked and acted on.

风险日志可以是一个 Google 文档、一块 Jira 看板，或一张电子表格；用什么都行，只要它被定期回顾。每个风险都被清晰描述、便于在对话中引用。缓解计划和当前状态保持可见，让团队里任何人都能快速了解进展。并且每个风险都有一个清晰的负责人——不一定是执行工作的人，但必须有人负责确保它被追踪、被处理。

For risks you’ve decided to accept, set a reminder to revisit them. Add a review date and use a system that will surface it back into your workflow.

对于你决定接受的风险，设一个提醒来重新检视它们。加上一个回顾日期，并用一套会把它重新带回你工作流的系统。

Don’t let this list get out of hand. Focus on the top-impact, high-likelihood risks. Keep it lean. A living document is valuable only if it stays useful.

别让这份清单失控。聚焦于影响最大、可能性最高的那些风险。保持精简。一份活文档，只有在它持续有用时才有价值。

Communicating risks沟通风险

The value of tracking risks comes from the conversations and actions that follow.

追踪风险的价值，来自随之而来的对话和行动。

The tricky thing is that not everyone sees risks the same way. A product owner might not care about a rare JSON parser vulnerability, but your security lead absolutely will.

棘手之处在于：不是每个人都以同样的方式看待风险。产品负责人可能不在乎一个罕见的 JSON 解析器漏洞，但你的安全负责人绝对在乎。

That’s why communication matters. When talking about risks, do it early, especially with supporters and decision makers. Don’t just surface the problem; come with a clear plan and a few alternatives. Focus on the impact: explain what could happen and why it matters. Be empathetic. Try to see things from their perspective: what would they worry about? And be honest. Don’t exaggerate to make a point, but also don’t downplay something important. Focus on facts.

这就是为什么沟通很重要。谈论风险时，要早谈，尤其是和支持者、决策者谈。别只把问题摆出来；要带着一个清晰的计划和几个备选方案。聚焦于影响：解释可能发生什么、以及它为什么重要。要有同理心。试着从他们的视角看问题：他们会担心什么？并且要诚实。别为了强调观点而夸大，但也别淡化重要的事情。聚焦于事实。

Managing risk is as much about alignment as it is about action. Use the tools and conversations described here to stay ahead of problems and to help people see clearly what’s coming.

管理风险，既关乎行动，也同样关乎对齐。用这里描述的工具和对话，抢先于问题一步，并帮助人们清晰地看到正在逼近什么。

Key Takeaway本章要点

Managing technical projects is about more than tracking tickets or hitting deadlines. It’s about creating clarity, reducing ambiguity, and helping your team move forward with focus.

管理技术项目，不只是追踪工单或赶上截止日期。它关乎创造清晰、减少模糊，并帮助团队带着专注向前。

From aligning on a shared strategy and defining a clear technical vision to making decisions efficiently and documenting them well, strong technical leadership gives your team the structure it needs to deliver.

从在共享战略上对齐、定义清晰的技术愿景，到高效地做决策并把决策记录好，强有力的技术领导为团队提供了交付所需的结构。

— PDF p.320 —

You won’t be able to plan for everything. But with the right habits—clear planning, fast feedback loops, ongoing measurement, and continuous communication—you’ll be able to keep projects on track, navigate complexity, and recover quickly when things go off course.

你不可能为一切都做好计划。但有了正确的习惯——清晰的规划、快速的反馈回路、持续的度量、以及不间断的沟通——你就能让项目不脱轨、驾驭复杂性，并在事情偏离正轨时迅速恢复。
